The inscription may be translated as: 

The first dew has just begun to fall, and coolness arises over the coastal land. Xiaoshan, Mr Xie, came from Kunling at dawn and presented to Ding this long hanging scroll depicting an ancient cypress. A longevity vine, extending a thousand xun in length, luxuriantly trails down beneath it. Below, a deer raises its head and gazes upward to receive it. The composition presumably takes the meaning of 'receiving the hundred blessings bestowed by Heaven.' The brushwork is vigorous yet moist, lively and animated, and conveys something of the secluded and profound spirit of the Yuan masters. To my venerable elder clansman Piweng, whose literary accomplishments and ability in affairs of state are extraordinary, and whose talent and character surpass those of ordinary men: I respectfully hope to see you follow your distinguished reputation, receive the gracious favour and promotion, and enjoy immeasurable blessings and emoluments. I, Ding, your younger kinsman, respectfully offer this painting, and hereby make it a token of our bond. On the third day after the Beginning of Spring, in the Xinwei year of the Qianlong era, Xiangshan Chen Bending respectfully inscribed this at the Chanyan Studio. Xiaoshan, Shen Guan

Xie Shenguan (謝身灌) was a Qing dynasty painter from Shan county, Henan Province, with the courtesy name of Xiaoshan. He was particularly proficient in landscape paintings. For further information, see Zhongguo jinxiandai shuhuajia cidian (中國近現代書畫家辭典), Tianjin, 2000, p.511.

Chen Bending (陳本鼎), a native of Xiangtan, Hunan Province, with the courtesy name of Xiangshan, served as Assistant Magistrate of Datong County (大同縣縣丞), Shanxi Province during the Qianlong reign. See Xiangtan lidai shicixuan shang (湘潭歷代詩詞選 上), Xiangtan, 2013, p.261.

See a 'deer' painting of similar theme and composition, signed by Shen Quan (1682-1760), Qing dynasty, in the collection of the Palace Museum, Beijing (acc.no.新00005575).

Hu Wenming is considered amongst the most accomplished artisans of the late Ming dynasty. The shape of the incense burner is based on an archaic prototype dating to the Shang or Zhou dynasties. The animated creatures, however, may have been drawn from the 'Classic of Mountains and Seas', Shan Hai Jing, compiled between the 2nd or 3rd centuries BC.

A bronze incense burner signed by Hu Wenming and decorated with mythical creatures, approx. 1550-1600, is illustrated in Power and Glory: Court Arts of China's Ming Dynasty, San Francisco, 2008, p.180, no.111. See also a parcel-gilt copper incense burner, gui, Yunjian Hu Wenming mark, late 16th/early 17th century, illustrated by R.Mowry, China's Renaissance in Bronze: The Robert H. Clague Collection of Later Chinese Bronzes, Phoenix, 1993, p.67. The exceptional quality of the present vessel is demonstrated in the various techniques, from the silver-wire inlay, to the chasing and engraving, as well as the parcel gilding.

A similar parcel-gilt silver-inlaid bronze incense burner, gui, Yunjian Hu Wenming mark, late 16th/early 17th century, was sold at Christie's Hong Kong, 27 November 2017, lot 8117.

A similar scene of a general approaching a lady, her hand raised within her sleeve, is depicted on a blue and white brushpot, Chongzhen, illustrated in Transitional Wares and Their Forerunners, Hong Kong, 1981, no.82. See also a blue and white beaker vase of similar form, with related decoration to the middle and lower sections, but with the upper section painted with birds amidst ornamental rocks and flowering sprays, illustrated in Ibid., Hong Kong, 1981, p.89, no.65. An inscription on the vase incorporates the cyclical date Gengchen (庚辰), corresponding to 1640.

The subject may tentatively relate to one of the celebrated tales of beautiful women whose allure brings about the downfall of powerful men. One possibility is the story of Xi Shi (西施), the renowned beauty whom Goujian (勾踐), King of Yue, sent to Fuchai (夫差), King of Wu, in an attempt to distract him from affairs of state; Fuchai became so enamoured of her that he neglected the government of his kingdom, ultimately contributing to its downfall. Alternatively, the scene may allude to the story of Diaochan (貂蟬), whose beauty was used to set the military commander Lü Bu (呂布) against his patron Dong Zhuo (董卓) in the Romance of the Three Kingdoms. Both narratives would have carried particular resonance in the late Ming, when such stories could be read not simply as romantic episodes but as cautionary tales concerning the disruptive power of beauty, desire and the femme fatale within the political sphere.

See a related blue and white vase, gu, circa 1640, which was sold at Christie's New York, 20 September 2013, lot 1317. See also a related blue and white beaker vase, gu, circa 1640, which was sold at Bonhams London, 12 May 2016, lot 39.

Whilst the decorative design of bajixiang and ruyi-lappet borders can be seen, for example, on Qianlong period bowls - this exact design on a Jiaqing period bowl is very rare. The Eight Auspicious Symbols are objects that symbolise Buddhist teachings. They consist of eight motifs (a wheel, conch shell, parasol, victory banner, lotus, vase, fish, and endless knot) each signifying good fortune and auspiciousness. This decorative motif was introduced from Tibetan Lamaism and first appeared during the Yuan dynasty, reaching its height of popularity during the Ming and Qing dynasties.

The decorative scheme of this dish may be distinctive to the Yongzheng Imperial kilns and is rare. The interior is finely painted with a ground of interlocking fangsheng (方勝) motifs, interspersed with five groups of ruyi clouds supporting peaches, an auspicious symbol of longevity. The fangsheng motif, a legendary hair ornament of the Queen Mother of the West, characterised by its symmetrical and balanced configuration of interlocking lozenges, conveys the auspicious meanings of unity, harmony, and shared purpose.

The considerable scale of the present lot, together with the precision of its potting and densely organised decoration, demonstrates the technical sophistication achieved at the Imperial kilns at Jingdezhen. The production and firing of such a substantial vessel demanded careful control, while the complex arrangement of motifs had to be planned across the broad, curved surface to achieve a balanced composition. The rich cobalt-blue further enhances the monumental character of the vase.

Earlier prototypes of the present design can be seen in the Yongzheng period. See, for example, a related blue and white hu, Yongzheng seal mark and of the period, decorated with the bajixiang but without shou characters within the lotus blooms, illustrated in Qing Imperial Porcelain of the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong Reigns, Hong Kong, 1995, no.44. By the Qianlong reign, the lotus blossoms are found with shou characters incorporated within their centres, as on the present vase. See a very similar blue and white hu with bajixiang decoration, Qianlong seal mark and of the period, illustrated in Chinese Porcelain: The S.C. Ko Tianminlou Collection, Hong Kong, 1987, pl.58, subsequently sold at Sotheby's Hong Kong, 2 April 2019, lot 16. Another very similar blue and white vase, Qianlong seal mark and of the period, is illustrated in Anthology of Chinese Art: Min Chiu Society Silver Jubilee Exhibition, Hong Kong, 1985, no.185. See also another similar vase, Qianlong seal mark and of the period, illustrated in Appreciation of Blue and White Porcelains, Taipei, 2008, pl.52. Another blue and white vase, Qianlong seal mark and of the period, was illustrated by A.du Boulay, Christie's Pictorial History of Chinese Ceramics, Oxford, 1984, p.202.

The present vase is distinguished by the sophisticated combination of an archaic hu form, early Ming inspired blue and white decoration and Tibetan Buddhist imagery. The arrangement of the bajixiang, each emblem positioned above a lotus bloom enclosing a shou character, is particularly striking. The Eight Buddhist Auspicious Emblems were introduced into Chinese decorative arts through Tibetan Buddhism and appear on Chinese blue and white porcelain from the Yuan dynasty onwards, initially more commonly as border decoration. During the Ming and Qing periods they became increasingly prominent as principal motifs, frequently combined with lotus. A related blue and white jar with lotus scrolls supporting the Eight Buddhist Emblems, Zhengtong, is illustrated in Blue and White Porcelain with Underglazed Red, vol.1, Hong Kong, 2000, p.189, no.178. The addition of shou characters in the lotus bloom introduces the auspicious wish for longevity into an otherwise Buddhist decorative scheme.

The unusual combination of lotus blooms enclosing shou characters is also found on a very similar blue and white vase, hu, Qianlong but without the Imperial reign mark, illustrated in Ethereal Elegance: Porcelain Vases of the Imperial Qing. The Huaihaitang Collection, Hong Kong, 2007, no.97. The recurrence of this motif on Imperial vessels suggests that the shou within lotus design formed part of the auspicious decorative repertoire of the Qianlong period Imperial kilns, combining the symbolism of longevity with the lotus, an important Buddhist and auspicious motif.

The archaistic form reflects the Qianlong Emperor's well known fascination with antiquity and, in particular, his study and collection of archaic bronzes, jades and other early works of art. The porcelain hu can be understood within the long Chinese tradition of translating ancient bronze forms into later materials, retaining the authority of the antique while allowing for new decorative possibilities. Here, the archaistic taotie mask handles reinforce the reference to bronze, while the 15th century-inspired blue and white decoration and bajixiang create a distinctly Qianlong period synthesis of antiquarian and contemporary Courtly taste.

The hu form remained in production throughout the Qing dynasty. A related smaller Qianlong period vase with a different decorative scheme, decorated with leafy lotus blooms, composite floral scrolls and a broad band of crashing waves, is in the Palace Museum, Taipei, and illustrated in Blue and White Ware of the Ch'ing Dynasty, Hong Kong, 1968, pl.2. A related blue and white lotus scroll vase, zun, Daoguang mark and of the period, is illustrated by Geng Baochang, Ming Qing ciqi jianding [Appraisal of Ming and Qing porcelains], Hong Kong, 1993, pl.510.

See a related but smaller (25cm high) blue and white floral hu vase, without bajixiang, Qianlong seal mark and of the period, which was sold at Sotheby's New York, 11 September 2019, lot 623. Compare also with a related blue and white hu vase, Qianlong seal mark and of the period, but smaller (25.4cm high) which was sold at Sotheby's New York, 21-22 September 2021, lot 77. See also a similar blue and white vase, Qianlong seal mark and of the period, of similar size (50cm high), which was sold at Sotheby's Hong Kong, 3-4 May 1994, lot 183.

The square box and cover are decorated with an elderly figure holding a ruyi (如意) fungus and a boy carrying a vase containing a three-pronged halberd (三戟). The ruyi, meaning 'as desired' or 'as one wishes', conveys the notion of fulfilment of one's wishes, while the three-pronged halberd forms a pun on sanjí (三戟), which is associated through homophony with 三級 ('three grades' or 'ranks'), expressing the wish for advancement in rank. Together, these motifs convey the auspicious wish for 'quick promotion as you wish'.

The square box and cover with canted corners depict an episode from the Romance of the Western Chamber (Xixiang ji 西廂記). The military commander Sun Feihu besieges the monastery in an attempt to abduct Miss Cui. Madam Cui promises that she will marry her daughter to whoever can repel the bandits. Eager to win the lady's hand, Zhang Sheng writes to his friend Du Que, the governor of Puzhou, seeking assistance, and entrusts the monk Huiming with delivering the letter and leaving the monastery to summon help.

The cicada-blade pattern carved above the waist reflects the Qianlong Court's pronounced taste for archaism, inspired by the geometric ornament of ancient bronze vessels and its adaptation to contemporary Court furniture. See, for example, an archaic bronze ritual vessel, gu with cicada blades around the mouth, Shang dynasty, in the British Museum, London (acc.no.1935,0115.21). Compare with a zitan table with stretchers and carved plantain-leaf pattern on the waist, Qianlong, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in The Complete Collection of Treasures of the Palace Museum: Furniture of the Ming and Qing (II), Hong Kong, 2002, p.121, no.106. See also a zitan table, the waist carved with pendant plantain-leaf lappets, Qing dynasty, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in Ibid., p.114, no.101. A zitan incense stand, Qianlong, also carved with cicada lappets, is in the Qing Court Collection, and illustrated in Ibid., no.151. 

By the Qianlong reign, zitan had become one of the most highly prized materials of the Qing Court. Its scarcity, slow growth and limited availability meant that existing stocks were carefully controlled by the Imperial Household Department, with much of the timber used at Court imported from Southeast Asia. The Qianlong Emperor showed particular favour for zitan, which was extensively employed in the Palace Workshops for furniture and decorative objects. Its exceptionally dense, fine-grained structure was particularly suited to elaborate carving, allowing the intricate archaistic decoration of the present table to be rendered with remarkable precision.

Compare with an Imperial zitan corner-leg table, Qianlong/Jiaqing, which was sold at Bonhams Hong Kong, 28 May 2019, lot 123. See also a rare narrow zitan side table, 17th/18th century, which was sold at Christie's New York, 16 March 2017, lot 642.

清乾隆/嘉慶 紫檀拼硬木髹金漆山水圖亮格櫃一對

Provenance: Evaristo Caretti (1879-1955), China and Italy, and thence by descent
Noted in a valuation conducted by Robert Kleiner in 1988, stating it was acquired in Beijing in 1924

來源： Evaristo Caretti (1879-1955)，中國及意大利，並由後人保存迄今
Robert Kleiner于1988年所作的評估中曾提及，此件拍品于1924年獲得于北京 

The present pair of cabinets are notable for the exceptionally fine quality of the carving, the use of richly figured zitan wood, and the lavish gilt-lacquer decoration, combining precious materials and elaborate craftsmanship to a dazzling effect. See a related veneered zitan, hongmu and lacquer display and book cabinet, late Qing dynasty, illustrated by Tian Jiaqing, Classic Chinese Furniture of the Qing Dynasty, Hong Kong, 1995, pp.236-237, no.107. 

Duobao ge (多寶格), literally 'multiple-treasure cabinets', developed during the Qing dynasty from earlier forms of Chinese display furniture, including the liangge gui of the Ming dynasty. In Qing palace inventories and archives, such cabinets were often described as bogu shuge (博古書格), literally 'cabinets for displaying antiquities and books', reflecting their dual function: the open compartments provided a setting for the display of antiquities and scholar's objects, while the enclosed lower sections were used to store books, scrolls and other possessions.

The Imperial Household Department archives contain numerous references to the design and production of such cabinets, including discussions by the Yongzheng and Qianlong Emperors concerning their form and decoration. The taste for lacquer, particularly Japanese lacquer, was also evident at the Qing Court. Both the Kangxi and Yongzheng Emperors showed a marked appreciation for Japanese lacquerware, and objects produced for the Court during their reigns also incorporated techniques and decorative styles derived from Japanese prototypes. See for example, a related zitan display cabinet with gilt-lacquer decoration, mid-Qing dynasty, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in The Complete Collection of Treasures of the Palace Museum: Furniture of the Ming and Qing Dynasties (II), Hong Kong, 2002, p.270, no.229. The combination of richly figured zitan, black-and-gilt lacquer and elaborate openwork carving as seen on the present pair reflects this broader Qing taste for combining precious materials and diverse decorative traditions within the scholar's interior.

The carved decoration of quatrefoil ruyi-shaped plantain leaves is particularly rare, the highly symmetrical arrangement and geometric conception being markedly unusual within the vocabulary of Chinese furniture ornament. At the centre is a four-pronged leaf form, surrounded diagonally by four further elongated, quatre-lobed plantain leaves, creating a distinctive rotational composition with an almost Islamic character. The design may reflect the influence of Mughal jade carving at the Qing Court, where four-petalled and open-flower forms, together with elaborate foliate ornament, provided a distinctive vocabulary of ornament. Compare, for example, the base of a Mughal jade foliate bowl, carved with a four-petalled flower, illustrated in Exquisite Beauty: Islamic Jades, Taipei, 2007, p.75, no.67; and p.126, no.152. Such forms may have provided an inspiration for the assimilation of Mughal floral and geometric vocabulary into Qing decorative arts, here imaginatively combined with the traditional Chinese motif of the plantain leaf. See also a jade vase, Qianlong six-character mark and of the period, with related geometric designs, illustrated in Oriental Works of Art, London, 1992, no.81.

Compare with a similar single gilt-lacquered zitan and hardwood display cabinet, 18th/19th century, which was sold at Christie's London, 11 May 2016, lot 369. Another similar gilt-lacquered zitan display cabinet, 18th century, was sold at Christie's Hong Kong, 29 May 2007, lot 1398.

By the Qing dynasty, zitan had become an exceptionally scarce and valuable timber. The slow growth of the tree, together with the depletion of mature timber, resulted in dwindling supplies, while much of the material available to the Qing Court was imported from Southeast Asia and its use carefully regulated. Its dense grain, hardness and natural lustre nevertheless made it particularly prized for furniture, especially where elaborate carving was required. The scarcity of large sections increasingly encouraged the use of zitan veneer, conserving the precious timber while retaining its characteristic colour, grain and lustrous surface.

Mid-Qing Dynasty
The top panel set within a rectangular frame above a high waist elaborately carved in relief with bamboo, plum blossoms and pine branches between lappet borders, elegantly scrolled lotus flowers and leaves further carved on the shaped aprons and extending down the legs, the whole supported on four legs of square section terminating in floral-shaped feet, the wood of an attractive dark chocolate hue. 121.9cm (48in) wide x 85.2cm (33 1/2in) high x 44cm (17 3/8in) deep.

Noted in a valuation conducted by Robert Kleiner in 1988

來源： Evaristo Caretti (1879-1955)，中國及意大利，並由後人保存迄今

Elaborately carved zitan furniture is particularly rare, owing to the difficulty of carving such a dense and valuable wood. For examples of related zitan tables, see one carved with a lingzhi pattern, Qing dynasty, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in The Complete Collection of Treasures of the Palace Museum. Furniture of the Ming and Qing Dynasties (II), Hong Kong, 2002, pl.100. See also a zitan table with similar treatment of the carved lotus patterns on the aprons and waist, Qianlong, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in Ibid., no.91. 

The elegantly scrolling lotus foliage on the aprons and legs also reflects the Qing dynasty taste for increasingly elaborate and naturalistic foliate ornament. During the Qianlong period, traditional Chinese floral motifs were sometimes rendered in conjunction with European-inspired scrolling foliage, particularly acanthus, introduced to the Qing court through Jesuit artists and European style interiors at the Yuanmingyuan. The flowing treatment of the lotus leaves on the present table recalls this broader taste for luxuriant foliate carving, while retaining the distinctly Chinese lotus motif; for more on European influence on Chinese furniture, see Tian Jiaqing, 'Zitan and Zitan Furniture', Chinese Furniture: Selected Articles from Orientations 1984-1999, Hong Kong, 1999, pp.195-196. See also related acanthus leaves carved on a zitan lotus-decorated stool, mid-Qing dynasty, illustrated by Tian Jiaqing, Classic Furniture of the Qing Dynasty, Hong Kong, 1995, p.81, no.15.

The 'Three Friends of Winter' (suihan sanyou, 歲寒三友) carved in relief across the waist, aprons and legs, are traditionally associated with resilience and steadfastness: pine and bamboo remain evergreen through winter, while prunus is celebrated for flowering in the coldest months. Together they came to symbolise endurance, integrity and friendship in adversity, and formed one of the most enduring auspicious themes in Chinese art. The incorporation of all three plants into a continuous, naturalistic composition across the table is particularly effective, with the gnarled branches and flowering stems contrasting with the dark, lustrous surface of the zitan. A zitan table carved with the 'Three Friends of Winter' is in the Art Institute of Chicago, bequest of Russell Tyson, (acc.no.1964.572).

A related zitan table carved with prunus, early 18th century, was sold at Sotheby's Hong Kong, 7 April 2010, lot 1847.

See a very similar small (180cm high) hongmu square-corner cabinet and hat chest, xiaosijiangui, mid-Qing dynasty, illustrated by Tian Jiaqing, Classical Chinese Furniture of the Qing Dynasty, Hong Kong, 1996, pp.220–223, no.100. The carved decoration of archaistic kui-dragons, bats, musical stones and double fish is closely related. The use of archaistic kui-dragons is characteristic of the mid-Qing taste for antiquity, reflecting a broader interest among the Qing scholarly elite in the study and reinterpretation of China's ancient past. This antiquarian interest was closely associated with the rise of kaozheng 考證 ('evidential scholarship'), which placed renewed emphasis on the examination of ancient texts, inscriptions and material remains, and contributed to a wider revival of archaic forms in the arts. Such motifs were not simply copied from antiquity, but reinterpreted within contemporary decorative schemes. Tian interprets the combination of bat (fu 蝠), musical stone (qing 磬) and double fish (shuangyu 雙魚) as the auspicious rebus fuqing youyu (福慶有餘), conveying the wish for 'endless rejoicing'. The same motif of bat, chime and double fish is carved on the back panel of a zitan armchair, mid to late Qing dynasty, illustrated in Ibid., no.37. 

Compound cabinets of this type were used principally for the storage of clothing, with the upper section providing additional space for hats and other smaller garments or personal possessions. Such wardrobes could be made on a monumental scale in wealthy households. In Cao Xueqin's novel Honglou meng (Dream of the Red Chamber), Granny Liu is astonished by the enormous wardrobes in the Jia household and wonders how their upper compartments could be reached, eventually realising that a ladder must be used. See, for example, a larger huanghuali compound cabinet (280cm high), Qing dynasty, illustrated by Chen Zengbi, A Teaching Legacy: Study on Ancient Chinese Furniture, Beijing, 2022, p.241.

The present cabinet is considerably more modest in scale, with its refinement and status instead expressed through the intricacy and labour-intensive nature of its carving. The carving is notable for its fine execution in relief, with twisted-rope borders and raised archaistic scrolls defined by sharply cut grooves and ridges. The careful separation of the raised ornament from the ground and the precise treatment of the narrow grooves give the decoration considerable clarity and depth despite the density of the composition. See related carving of archaistic kui-dragons on the lower zitan panels of a sixteen-leaf screen with Luohans, Qianlong, illustrated in The Emperor's Private Paradise: Treasures from the Forbidden City, New Haven and Yale, 2011, p.165, pl.49.

Compare with a similar large pair of hongmu compound cabinets, sijiangui, 19th century, sold at Christie's Hong Kong, 31 May 2010, lot 2047.

See a related zitan chair, densely carved with lotus, Qing dynasty, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in The Complete Collection of Treasures of the Palace Museum: Furniture of the Ming and Qing Dynasties (II), Hong Kong, 2002, p.66, no.55.

The unusually small scale of the present chair raises the possibility that it was intended for ceremonial rather than domestic use. Its elaborate five-clawed dragon decoration and throne-like form may suggest a symbolic seat associated with ancestral or religious display, perhaps intended to accommodate or represent an ancestral tablet rather than a living sitter. This possibility may be further supported by the Qianlong reign mark on the incised and gilt back. See a gold lacquered wood spirit throne and footrest with memorial tablet, c.1800, illustrated in Splendors of China's Forbidden City: The Glorious Reign of Emperor Qianlong, Hong Kong, 2004, p.270, no.351.

The carving of the present lot is notable for its combination of Imperial and archaistic motifs. The central back panel is dominated by a five-clawed dragon amidst ruyi clouds, above crashing waves and rocky outcrops. The five-clawed dragon was closely associated with the emperor and Imperial authority, while the dragon above waves and mountains forms an established Imperial decorative vocabulary, evoking the ruler's dominion over the realm. See a zitan bed carved with similar crashing waves against rocks, but beneath lotus, early Qing dynasty, illustrated in The Complete Collection of Treasures of the Palace Museum: Furniture of the Ming and Qing Dynasties (II), Shenzhen, 2002, pp.4-5, no.2.

The ruyi clouds are auspicious, expressing the wish for all things to proceed 'as desired'. See related carving of clouds on a zitan table, Qianlong, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in Ibid., no.135. The lotus carved above the central panel is likewise an auspicious Buddhist motif associated with purity. The side panels and armrests are carved with highly stylised archaistic kui dragons, their angular bodies and scrolling forms derived from archaic bronzes, reflecting the Qing Court's antiquarian taste. See related carving of kui dragons on a zitan bed, Qing dynasty, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in The Complete Collection of Treasures of the Palace Museum: Furniture of the Ming and Qing Dynasties (II), Hong Kong, 2002, p.18, no.12.

The present lot is a superb example of the aesthetic taste of Palace furnishings produced during the Qianlong reign. In contrast to the Yongzheng Emperor's preference for nanmu, the Qianlong Emperor demonstrated a marked affinity for zitan, whose dense grain, rich purplish-brown tonality and exceptional durability made it particularly suited to the creation of lavish Imperial furnishings. The intricate ornamentation and elaborate carvings seen in the present lot reflect the Qianlong Emperor's love for opulence and exemplify the elaborate style of Qing Court furniture. By no later than the tenth year of the Qianlong period (1745), zitan furniture had become increasingly prevalent at the Qing Court. After the Qianlong reign, however, the production of zitan furniture for the Imperial Court underwent a marked decline. For further discussion, see Ge Fang, 'An Exploration of the Rise and Decline of Zitan Furniture in the Imperial Court during the Mid-Qing Period' (清中期宮廷紫檀家具之興衰探析), Art Journal (美術學報), 2018(6), 96-102.

The motifs on the present lot form a compound of auspicious symbolism. The Chinese word for bat, fu (蝠), is a homophone of fu (福), meaning 'blessing,' while the peach is traditionally associated with longevity. Together, bats and peaches express the wish for blessings and longevity, known as fu shou shuangquan (福壽雙全). The swastika emblem, also known as wan (萬 which means 'ten thousand') character motif, a Buddhist auspicious symbol, further enhances this symbolism. The combination of bats, peaches, and the wan motif conveys the auspicious wish for 'Ten Thousand Blessings and Ten Thousand Years of Longevity' (萬福萬壽).

Compare with a related hexagonal 'phoenix and dragon' zitan stool, Qianlong period, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in The Complete Collection of the Ming and Qing Dynasties: Furniture of the Ming and Qing Dynasties II (故宮博物館藏文物珍品全集：明清家具下), Hong Kong, 2002, p.92, no.81. Another related hexagonal zitan stool, but with straight sides, mid-Qing dynasty, in the Qing Court Collection, is illustrated in Ibid., no.71.

See a related Imperial zitan stool, Qianlong period, which was sold at Christie's Hong Kong, 4 October 2016, lot 61.

來源：Tim O'Donovan (1932-2025)，英國

Tim O'Donovan (1932-2025) was an Irish-born royal chronicler who spent more than four decades meticulously cataloguing the official engagements of the British Royal Family. A retired executive in the printing and paper industries, he turned his passion for detail into an annual statistical analysis of royal duties, compiling data from the Court Circular in leather-bound ledgers that became a uniquely authoritative—and at times controversial—record of royal work patterns.

The present lot is notable for its Yuanmingyuan mark on the base of the box, which may be translated as Fourth section of the Yuanmingyuan. Yuanmingyuan (圓明園, Garden of Perfect Brightness), also known as the Old Summer Palace, was a complex of Imperial gardens and palaces located in Haidian District, Beijing, China. It was constructed and expanded throughout the 18th and early 19th centuries, serving as the main Imperial residence of the Yongzheng Emperor and his four successors. Celebrated for its magnificent gardens and vast collections of Imperial art and treasures, the complex was devastated by British and French forces during the Second Opium War (1856–1860).

Compare with an Imperial cloisonné enamel vase which was sold at Bonhams London, 12 May 2011, lot 437, which bears incised marks in a format comparable to those found on the present lot. The inscription is arranged in two lines: the upper line is the Qianlong six-character reign mark, while the lower line reads Jianfu gong dier fen (建福宮第二分), which may be translated as 'Second Section of the Palace of Accumulated Blessings'.

Of square section and tall archaistic form, the neck and flaring foot each decorated with upright and pendant lappet bands enclosing a kui-dragon amid ruyi-head clouds, the neck further decorated with a panel enclosing a dragon above the mid-section, decorated with taotie masks, all against a turquoise ground, each face centred and edged by flanges, the sides of which are decorated with slender bands of floral sprays, the interior of the rim with a wide band of scrolling lotus. 52.5cm (20 3/4in) high.

The present lot is modelled after an archaic bronze form, the fanggu, a ritual wine vessel originating in the Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC). Its angular profile, flanged decoration and taotie patterns, reflect the enduring fascination with archaism that permeated Qing dynasty artistic production. From the late 17th century and early 18th century onwards, the Imperial Court actively encouraged the revival of ancient forms, with bronzes of the Shang and Zhou dynasties serving as direct models for works in porcelain, cloisonné enamel, and other media. Such pieces not only embodied a reverence for antiquity but also symbolised the continuity of ritual traditions and dynastic legitimacy.

See a similar cloisonné enamel vase, second half 17th century, illustrated in H.Brinker and A.Lutz, Chinesisches Cloisonné: Die Sammlung Pierre Uldry, Zurich, 1985, pl.178. See also related cloisonné enamel fanggu vases, early Qing dynasty, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in Compendium of Collections in the Palace Museum: Enamels, 2, Beijing, 2011, nos.36-39.

See a related but smaller cloisonné enamel vase, gu, 17th century, which was sold at Bonhams Hong Kong, 29 May 2023, lot 849.

Neolithic to Republic Period
Comprising: a strand of jade carvings including a dragon-form plaque, an ovoid bead encircled by a chi dragon in high relief and a tubular bead; a plaque carved on one side with a mythical beast mask, the reverse pierced with two apertures, attached to a cord strung with two beads; an ovoid bead carved in relief with a sinuous chi dragon and a plain ovoid bead, both attached to a cord strung with three small beads; a cord suspending a jade carving of a wengzhong figure, and two turtle-shell-form jade beads; a string attached with a jade rectangular pendant and a tubular jade bead; a white and russet jade carving of a dragonfly attached to a cord strung with a tubular bead; two white and black jade turtle-shell-shaped pendants; two drum-shaped jade beads; a russet jade carving of a wengzhong figure; two jade beads both carved in relief with scrolling clouds; a jade bead carved on each side with a taijitu; a greyish jade vajra. The largest, 5.3cm high. (15).

新石器時代至民國 玉珠及佩等玉飾一組

Wengzhong figures emerged as a distinctive type of jade ornament during the Han dynasty. According to tradition, Ruan Wengzhong 阮翁仲 was a formidable general who served under the First Emperor of Qin and was stationed at the frontier, where his imposing presence was said to have caused the invading Xiongnu to flee. Following his death, his likeness was reputedly cast in bronze as a protective figure, and during the Han dynasty small jade figures of Wengzhong were produced as personal ornaments, worn as pi-xie 辟邪 amulets to ward off evil and misfortune. A number of Han dynasty jade Wengzhong pendants are preserved in the Palace Museum, Beijing, illustrated in Compendium of Collections in the Palace Museum: Jade (故宮博物院藏品大系玉器編), vol.4, Beijing, 2011, pls.171-182. The type continued to be reproduced in later periods. Compare a Qing dynasty jade Wengzhong figure in the Palace Museum, Taipei (acc.no.故玉001909N000000000), and a Republic period example (acc.no.贈玉000251N000000000).

Compare the turtle-shell-shaped pendants with a related one, Western Zhou dynasty, in the collection of the Palace Museum, Beijing, illustrated in Chinese Jades in Traditional Collections (中國傳世玉器全集), vol.1, Beijing, 2010, p.166.

Neolithic Period and later
Comprising forty-four elongated pendants of varied form, carved from jade and hardstones of differing tones ranging from pale white to russet, dark brown and jasper-red, each pierced for suspension. The largest, 8.5cm (3 1/4in) long. (44).

新石器時代及其後 玉錐形器一組 

The awl-shaped jade ornaments as seen in the present lot may originally have been tools used to scrape the acupuncture points of the human body for therapeutic purposes, gradually developing into ornaments imbued with the significance of communicating with the divine. In Liangzhu burials, these awl-shaped jade ornaments are often found with their pointed ends facing upward above the head of the deceased. They may have been sewn onto or fastened to a headdress through the small perforations. See further discussion and four related awl-shaped jade ornaments, Liangzhu Culture, c.3300-2300 BC, in the collection of the Palace Museum, Taipei, illustrated in Select Jades in the Palace Museum: The Spirit of Jade, I (故宮玉器精選全集：玉之靈I), Taipei, 2019, p.373. 

See one related awl-shaped jade ornament, Shixia Culture, c.2500-1500 BC, excavated from Shixia site at Maha, Shaoguan, Guangdong Province, in the Guangdong Provincial Museum and illustrated by Gu Fang, The Complete Collection of Jades Unearthed in China (Zhongguo chutu yuqi quanji), vol.11, Beijing, 2005, p.21.

商晚期/西周早期至清代 玉魚 一組十二件

Fish (yu 魚) are among the most auspicious motifs in Chinese art. As the word for fish is a homophone for 'surplus' or 'abundance' (yu 餘), fish symbolise prosperity, wealth, and the wish for continual plenty: nian nian you yu (年年有餘, 'may there be abundance year after year').

Compare the white jade fish pendant to a similar one, Ming dynasty, illustrated by Gu Fang, The Complete Collection of Jades Unearthed in China (中國出土玉器全集), vol.1, Beijing, 2005, p.71. See also three related pendants in the shape of a fish, late Shang dynasty, illustrated in ibid., vol.4, p.53, p.72 and p.135. Compare the fish pendant with five beads on the string to a similar jade 'fish' pendant, excavated from tomb no.222 at Qianzhangda, Tengzhou, Shandong Province, illustrated in ibid., p.155. See also a related jade 'fish' pendant, Western Zhou dynasty, excavated from Tomb no.7 at Hejia-zhuanchang, Qishan, Shaanxi Province, illustrated by Gu Fang, The Complete Collection of Jades Unearthed in China, vol.14, Beijing, 2005, p.57. See also three more jade 'fish' plaques, Western Zhou dynasty, illustrated in ibid., vol.15, pp.72-75. 

See a similar celadon jade 'fish' pendant, late Ming/Qing dynasty, which was sold at Sotheby's Hong Kong, 30 November 2016, lot 102. See also a yellow jade fish-form pendant, Ming dynasty, which was sold at Christie's Hong Kong, 28 May 2014, lot 3658.

Eastern Zhou Dynasty
Of gently arched form, each terminal carved as a dragon head, the central section decorated with spiral bosses, the stone of pale green tone with russet and beige inclusions, fitted box. 11.2cm (4 3/8in) wide. (2).

東周 青玉龍紋璜

Prior to the Warring States period, jade huang pendants were generally worn as individual ornaments. They were perforated only at the two ends, with the concave side of the arc facing upward when worn. After the Warring States period, however, many jade huang were worn as components of composite jade pendants. To facilitate this new mode of suspension, an additional perforation was drilled into the convex edge as seen in the present lot, enabling the pendant to be mounted with the convex side uppermost as part of a larger assemblage. For further discussion, see Zhou Nanquan, 'Yuhuang zonglun' (玉璜綜論), in Palace Museum Journal, 1996(3), pp.8-22, p.14. 

While many scholars continue to identify pieces like the present lot as huang, others classify the ones suspended with the convex side uppermost as heng (珩), regarding them as a later development of the huang (璜). See a composite jade pendant set including a heng, Han dynasty, in the collection of the Xuzhou Museum, illustrated in An Epic of Chinese Jade for 10,000 Years (玉潤中華：中國玉器的萬年史詩圖卷), Nanjing, 2023, p.247.

See a related pair of 'twin dragon head' pendants, huang, Warring States period, which was sold at Sotheby's Paris, 12 December 2025, lot 134.

或為周及其後 玉勒子、環及虎符等 一組五件
款識：（一）君佩奇珍，良玉爲寶，共推三代，玩賞宜人。
（二）虎符

The inscription on the jade tiger mask ornament reads hufu (虎符) meaning 'tiger tally.' The term derives from ancient bronze tiger-shaped tallies that served as credentials for granting military authority upon officials and authorising the mobilisation of troops.

The inscription on the white jade bead, lezi, may be translated as: 

You wear a rare treasure; fine jade is its precious substance. Together it evokes the Three Dynasties, delightful to admire and appreciate.

東周或其後 玉環及瑗 一組七件

Although there is a traditional view that all jade discs with a central aperture are bi as can be seen in some archaeological reports, some scholars, including Zhou Nanquan, argue that these objects should be classified more carefully according to the definitions in historical records. According to the 'Explanation of Ritual Objects' (釋器) chapter of the Han dynasty lexicon Approach to Correct (爾雅): 'When the width of the rim is twice the diameter of the central hole, it is called a bi. When the diameter of the central hole is twice the width of the rim, it is called a yuan. When the width of the rim and the diameter of the central hole are equal, it is called a huan' (肉倍好謂之璧，好倍肉謂之瑗，肉好若一謂之環). For further discussion of this topic, see Zhou Nanquan, 'Lun Zhongguo gudai de yuqi' (論中國古代的玉璧), Palace Museum Journal, 1991(1), pp.76-88. 

Compare with a related jade disc, Eastern Zhou dynasty, excavated from the Donghaizi site, Jilin Province, now in the collection of the Ji'an Museum, illustrated in The Complete Collection of Jades Unearthed in China (中國出土玉器全集), vol.2, Beijing, 2005, p.181.

The discs of varying sizes and proportions, carved from stones displaying a broad range of natural colours and inclusions, from pale grey and green to warm beige and deep russet, two with raised collars. The largest, 6.3cm (2 1/2in) diam. (9).

或為東周/漢及以後 玉璧、環及瑗 一組九件

Jade bi, huan, and yuan were important objects in ancient China, each carrying distinctive ritual and social significance. According to the late Warring States period text Xunzi (荀子), 'Consult a worthy gentleman with a bi; summon a person with a yuan; dismiss a person with a jue; recall one who has been dismissed with a huan' (問士以璧，召人以瑗，絕人已玦，反絕以環). This passage illustrates how different jade forms functioned as material symbols of specific social relationships and ceremonial practices.

See a related jade disc, Spring and Autumn period, excavated from the tomb of Duke Qin of Jing, Shanxi Province, in the collection of Emperor Qinshihuang's Mausoleum Site Museum, Xi'an, and a jade disc, Warring States period, excavated from Fengxiang County, Shaanxi Province, in the collection of Shaanxi Provincial Institute of Archaeology, both illustrated in Eastern Zhou Jade Objects Excavated in Shaanxi (陝西出土東周玉器), Beijing, 2006 p.66 and p.182.

See two related jade discs, Warring States period/Han dynasty or later, which were sold at Bonhams London, 1 November 2021, lot 457. See also a group of nine mottled green and brown jade bi discs, which was sold at Christie's London, 7 December 2018, lot 662 (part lot).

漢代 豬玉握一件及玉塞兩件

A number of jade pig carvings in pairs were unearthed in tombs dated to the Han dynasty. People of the Han dynasty believed that the dead should not depart empty-handed; accordingly, such jade objects were placed in the hands of the deceased. A pig-shaped jade hand-held object symbolised wealth and good fortune. Comprising eight jade cicadas of varying sizes, each carved in a stylised form with the wings articulated by fine incised lines, the bodies and heads defined with simplified forms and eyes, the stones of assorted tones ranging from beige and pale celadon to deep brown and black, some with russet inclusions and natural markings. Jade cicadas have been highly esteemed in Chinese art since antiquity. They were traditionally placed on the tongue of the deceased as symbols of transformation and rebirth, inspired by the insect's emergence from the earth after years underground. The cicada was also later associated with purity and the virtues of the scholar, as its life high in trees and reliance on dew were seen as metaphors for moral refinement.

12th-14th century
The deity carved with hollow eyes and mouth beneath a tall headdress, the hands raised before the chest, the back with incised wings, the stone of pale greyish tone with dark brown patches. 3.1cm (1 1/4in) long.

十二至十四世紀 玉雕迦樓羅

Garuda (Jialouluo 迦楼罗) is a powerful mythical bird that entered Chinese visual culture through Buddhism, where it appears among the Eight Classes of Supernatural Beings as a fierce protector and enemy of the nagas (serpent beings). In Buddhist cosmology it embodies swiftness, strength, and the triumph of enlightened forces over poisonous or chaotic energies, often shown with outstretched wings and a predatory, eagle-like form. Originating in Indian mythology as the mount of Vishnu, Garuda was gradually absorbed into Chinese Buddhist iconography, where he appears in sculpture and esoteric imagery, particularly from the Tang period onward. In jade carvings of the Liao/Jin dynasty, the subject is rare and significant, reflecting the transmission of Himalayan and Central Asian Buddhist motifs into Chinese material culture, where such hybrid divine beings were associated with protection, spiritual power, and the subjugation of malevolent forces. See three related jade Garudas, Liao/Jin dynasty, in the collection of the Tianjin Museum, illustrated in Jade Wares Collected by Tianjin Museum (天津博物館藏玉), Tianjin, 2012, pp.164-167.

See a celadon and russet jade carving of a winged mythical figure, possibly Garuda, Yuan dynasty or earlier, which was sold at Sotheby's Hong Kong, 1 December 2016, lot 761.

description_block:
A DISTINGUISHED COLLECTION OF JADE CARVINGS é¡¯èµ«çå¨æ¶èA RARE WHITE JADE CARVING OF A RECUMBENT BOY
Song/Ming Dynasty
Carved as a crawling boy, the head turned to the left with a joyful facial expression, the arms tucked beneath his chest and grasping a small ball in the hands, the legs playfully bent up, with an aperture to the back for suspension, the stone of a white tone with cloudy inclusions. 4.5cm (1 3/4in) long.

宋/明 白玉戲球童子

The popularity of 'boy-at-play' motifs across a wide range of media, such as in the present lot, was rooted in the traditional Chinese belief that 'the more sons, the more blessings.' In addition, prevailing social customs created a strong demand for objects in the form of boy figures. A notable example is the celebration of the Qiqiao Festival (乞巧節), held on the seventh day of the seventh lunar month. On this occasion, households set out incense altars and performed rituals in which figures of children, known as mohouluo (摩睺羅), were often displayed. The term mohouluo derives from Buddhism, where it refers to the son of Siddhartha Gautama before his enlightenment as the Buddha. Mohouluo is renowned for his innate intelligence and pre-eminence in esoteric practice. Originally, such child figures served as ritual objects associated with prayers for male offspring and familial prosperity. Over time, they evolved into popular seasonal festival toys and customary gifts.

See a related jade carving of a recumbent boy grasping a ball, Jin dynasty, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in Compendium of Collections in the Palace Museum: Jade 5 (故宮博物院藏品大系：玉器編5), Beijing, 2011, p.212, no.250. Compare with a related white jade 'boy and drum' group, Song/Yuan dynasty, which was sold at Bonhams London, 16 May 2019, lot 202.

Song/Ming Dynasty
Skilfully carved as a long, crescent-shaped body terminating in a pointy tip, surmounted by a mythical beast head detailed with bulging eyes and pierced at the top for suspension, the reverse side incised with an eight-character inscription, the stone of white tone with russet patches. 5.5cm (2 1/8in) high.

宋/明 白玉帶皮獸面紋玉觿
款識：天地人 文仲子寶 祀 

The inscription may be translated as: 

Heaven, Earth, and Humanity; the treasured object of Wen Zhongzi; for sacrificial rites.

The Wen Zhongzi (文仲子) mentioned in the inscription is most likely Wang Tong 王通 (584-617), the Sui dynasty philosopher and politician who was posthumously honoured by his disciples with the title 'Wen Zhongzi'. A devoted advocate of Confucianism, Wang Tong emphasised the inseparable relationship between Heaven, Earth, and Humanity, regarding them as the three indispensable powers that together constitute the cosmos. He further reformulated the traditional cosmological concept of the Three Powers by assigning each a distinct ontological attribute: 'Heaven governs the primordial qi, Earth governs the primordial form, and Humanity governs the primordial consciousness' (天統元氣，地統元形，人統元識).

See a related yellowish-celadon jade pendant, xi, Ming dynasty, which was sold at Sotheby's Hong Kong, 18 December 2024, lot 6854.

Deftly carved as a crouching lion with its head turned slightly to the right, detailed with raised brows and a bushy mane, the body resting on its haunches with the forelegs bent, supported on a flat, square plinth pierced with two apertures, the stone of a white tone with beige and russet patches. 4.5cm (1 3/4in) long.

唐/遼 玉狻猊

The beast depicted in the present lot may be identified as a suanni (狻猊), a mythical creature whose earliest literary reference appears in the Warring States period Tale of King Mu, Son of Heaven (穆天子傳), which mentions: 'Among the famous beasts, some are capable of travelling a thousand li; the suanni and wild horses can travel five hundred li.' The Jin dynasty scholar Guo Pu commented: 'Suanni is the lion, native to the Western Regions.' In traditional Chinese mythology, the suanni is regarded as the fifth of the Nine Sons of the Dragon and is conventionally depicted as resembling a lion as seen in the present lot, a motif particularly seen in the art of the Tang dynasty. Carved in the form of a bird with its head facing forward, the wings folded neatly and incised with feathers, the legs tucked beneath the body, the stone of a greyish tone with brown and russet inclusions, attached to a cord strung with a cong-shaped bead and an ovoid bead. 5.2cm (2in) wide.

宋/明 玉鳩鳥；或為宋或以後 琮形及卵形玉飾

The bird depicted in the present lot may be identified as a turtledove (鳩 jiu). As early as the pre-Qin period, the turtledove already carried connotations of caring for and supporting the elderly. The Rites of Zhou (周禮) records that 'jiu were captured and respectfully offered as food for the senior elders of the state' (獻鳩以養國老). Sima Biao of the Western Jin dynasty, in his Treatise to the Book of the Later Han (《後漢書志》), explains that 'The jiu is a bird that does not choke. It is presented with the wish that the elderly may likewise never choke.'

Jade turtledove carvings were popular during the Han dynasty. A possible prototype may be seen in the Qing Court Collection, in the Palace Museum, Taipei (故玉005827N000000000). Zigang shan seal mark, Qing Dynasty
Exquisitely carved with a rectangular sections carved in low-relief with a calligraphic inscription and seal reading Zigang shan, terminating with a loop formed as an archaistic dragon biting its tail, the stone of even white tone. 5.9cm (2 5/8in) high.

清 白玉詩文提攜 
款識：白鶴長隨不老仙「子岡山」

The inscription may be translated as: 

The white crane remains eternally beside the ageless Immortal.

Lu Zigang (陸子岡, active 16th century) was the most celebrated jade carver of the Ming dynasty, renowned for his refined plaques and pendants produced in Suzhou. His works embodied the literati ideals of the period, combining the techniques of jade carving with the aesthetics of calligraphy and painting through elegant forms, finely incised decoration and poetic inscriptions. His reputation was such that his name became synonymous with the highest standards of jade craftsmanship. During the Qing dynasty, jade carvers frequently adopted the Zigang signature or produced works in the 'Zigang style' as a tribute to his artistic legacy, reflecting continued admiration for the Ming literati tradition rather than necessarily indicating direct authorship by the master himself. See a jade plaque, Zigang mark, in the Palace Museum, Beijing (acc.no.xin00042202). Another jade plaque, Zigang seal marks, late Qing dynasty/Republic, is in the Palace Museum, Taipei (acc.no.贈玉000264N000000000).

The present lot is a tixie (提攜) a term that may be translated literally as 'to take up'. It was an ancient type of belt fitting worn at the waist and used to suspend accessories such as sachets and jade pendants. See a related jade belt ornament, tixie, Yuan/Ming dynasty, in the Qing Court Collection, the Palace Museum, Taipei (acc.no.故玉002216N000000000). Suzhou, 18th/19th century 
Exquisitely carved with the cowherd standing atop a large ox crossing a bridge with finely incised hairs, the body cleverly highlighted in tones of russet and dark brown, the weaver girl above on a cloud with six crows arching around the left of the pendant to form a bridge connecting them, the reverse with calligraphic inscription issuing from a cloud, a sage below floating on a raft above waves, later 18ct-gold clasp. 5.1cm (2in) long.

十八/十九世紀 蘇作瑪瑙巧雕鵲橋相會圖詩文佩 
款識：天缘巧月渡銀河

Provenance: Spink & Son Ltd., London

來源：倫敦古董商Spink & Son Ltd.，
英國私人收藏，從上處獲得于1960年11月16日，並由後人保存迄今 

The present lot is notable for the exceptional quality of its carving and the skilful exploitation of the natural layers and tonal variations of the agate. The carver has used the contrasting russet, amber, cream and dark brown tones to distinguish the figures, ox and landscape, while the deeply undercut modelling gives the composition a remarkable sense of three-dimensionality. Particularly impressive is the use of the darker inclusions for the six crows, which arc around the pendant to form a visual bridge between the Cowherd and Weaver Girl, while the finely incised details of the ox's hair and the delicate clouds and waves demonstrate the precision of the carving.

The story of the Weaver Girl and the Cowherd (Zhinü and Niulang) depicted on the present lot, is one of China's most beloved romantic legends, celebrated during the Qixi Festival, often called the Chinese Valentine's Day. According to the tale, Zhinü was a celestial weaver, daughter of the Jade Emperor, who descended to earth and fell in love with the humble cowherd Niulang. They married and lived happily, but when the heavens discovered their union, the goddess of heaven separated them by creating the Milky Way across the sky. Moved by their devotion, a flock of magpies, sometimes described as black crows in regional versions, took pity on the lovers and formed a bridge with their wings once a year, on the seventh day of the seventh lunar month, allowing the two to reunite. The image of these dark-winged birds bridging the stars has come to symbolise love's perseverance and the tenderness of reunion after separation. 

The inscription on the reverse may be translated as:

By celestial destiny, the moon traverses the Milky Way

Yang Yanping studied architecture at Tsinghua University, graduating in 1958, continuing her studies at the Oil Painting Department of the Beijing Art Academy. In 1986, Yang and her husband, Zeng Shanqing, were awarded fellowships from the State University of New York at Stony Brook.

Her work can be found in leading worldwide museums, including: The Art Institute of Chicago which has recently held a major exhibition of her work, see Expressive Ink: Paintings by Yang Yanping and Zeng Shanqing, Chicago, 2019; the Art Museum of Beijing Fine Art Academy, Beijing; the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford; the Albertina, Vienna; the Asian Art Museum, San Francisco; the British Museum, London; and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. A major retrospective of her work was held at the Art Museum of Beijing Fine Art Academy in 2013.

Her depictions of Autumnal lotus flowers are her most definitive works, which stray close to pure abstraction, the lotus flower being a symbol of purity, transience, the fragility of nature, and the potential for regeneration. For a related painting by Yang Yanping, 'Deep Autumn', 2004, see China Onward: The Estella Collection, Chinese Contemporary Art, 1966-2006, Humlebaek, 2007, pp.360-361.

description_block:
YI MING (b.1974)
Dawning: Where Night's Last Dew Meets First Light, 2012
Oil on canvas, signed by the artist and dated 2012, framed.
70cm (27 5/8in) high x 50cm (19 3/4in) wide.

易茗（1974年生）白露未晞，東方將明：入澄明之境 2012年作 布面油畫 有框 
款識：ym2012 

The oil paintings of Yi Ming are perhaps his most important artistic contribution in a career bejewelled with significant achievements that include becoming Chief Image Designer for both the 2008 Beijing Olympic Games and the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympic Games, alongside work in film art direction and fashion criticism.

The present work is part of his important oeuvre of paintings that synthesise Eastern spiritual sensibility and Western abstract expressionism. It draws upon the ancient Chinese aesthetic principle of 'leaving blank space' (留白) in traditional Chinese landscape painting. His direct dialogue with Western abstract expressionism is given further nuance when viewed in the context of the visual language created by 20th century masters Zao Wou-Ki (1920–2013) and Chu Teh-Chun (1920–2014).

These artists began the process of marrying spatial and philosophical conception of Chinese landscape painting with Western abstract expressionism exploring the intersection of calligraphic, colour and light. In Yi's work we see something of the depth and emptiness of Zao married with the colour and rhythm of Chu.

We also see a masterful play with traditional Chinese artistic form. The vertical format of the work recalls the multi-perspective landscapes paintings, made for the hanging scroll format, during the Classical era of Chinese paintings. The eye is drawn effortlessly from bottom to top, and deep inside the 'imaginary landscape' which is afforded a gravity and monumentality by the layering of spirited brushstrokes in rich oils, in place of the more traditional medium of ink.

One of the striking attributes of the current work is its rich purple palette, which through modulations between black and white, mediates between themes of past and present, emptiness and plenty, and these, taken together, evoke the creative power of the elements earth, wind and water. 

The juxtaposition of the tight defined brushwork of dark fissures, with ephemeral cloud-like sweeps of white and purple, allows the viewer to inhabit both of these dichotomies simultaneously, uncertain as to which overlays the other. The viewer may thereby break free from the painting's grounding in nature to a multifaceted mental world of unrestricted possibilities. The title of the work 'Dawning' turns the natural phenomenon of the 'dawn' into a verb, an action. On one level this is a personification of nature, by injecting it with human agency. On another, it is a process of imbuing human thought with the potential of nature, which ultimately allows the viewer to experience the depth and profundity of the artist's creative world through the potential of a future emerging from the darkness of the past.

Compare to a related work by Yi Ming, Wind Whispers, which was sold at China Guardian Hong Kong, 7 April 2025, lot 89; and another work by the artist, sold at Rongbao Zhai, Beijing, 18-19 June 2024, lot 1572.

款識：鸥集湘庭，云碧龙映樽；凤栖明潭，霞橙帘梳月。辛卯年秋宋莊魏舘 剛記

Provenance: acquired directly from the artist

The inscription may be translated as:

Gulls gather by the Xiang courtyard, emerald clouds reflecting the dragon in the wine cup; Phoenixes perch beside the bright pool, orange clouds comb the moonlight through the curtains. Written in the autumn of the Xinmao year, at the Wei Pavilion in Songzhuang, recorded by Gang.

Wei Ligang 魏立剛 was born in Datong, Shanxi Province. At the age of 17, he entered the Mathematics Department of Nankai University, where he developed the rigorous logical and analytical skills that would later inform his artistic practice. During his university years, he served as president of the university's calligraphy society, studying classical poetry and epigraphic scripts under the supervision of the local masters Li Henian (1912-2000), Wang Xuezhong (1925-2013), and Sun Boxiang (1934-). After graduating from Nankai University in 1985, Wei Ligang became a teacher in Taiyuan and immersed himself in the legacy of Fu Shan (1607-1684), the renowned calligrapher and art theorist during the late Ming and early Qing dynasties. From the mid-1990s onward, he increasingly engaged with abstract painting and international contemporary art. During the 1990s, he emerged as a leading young practitioner of modern calligraphy, participating in and organising a number of influential exhibitions that helped shape the movement.

Wei Ligang has continually expanded the expressive possibilities of calligraphy, pushing the medium beyond the boundaries of conventional script. His eclectic sources of inspiration encompass ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs, industrial civilisation and modern machinery, European castles and palaces, contemporary physics and astronomy, as well as the structures and forms of plants and animals. In the present lot, elegant black lines move fluidly across a luminous gold ground, combining the spontaneous, gestural energy of abstract expressionism with the archaic grid-like structure of Chinese writing. The result is a dynamic synthesis of calligraphic tradition and contemporary abstraction.

Wei Ligang's works held in numerous major institutional and private collections, including the Asian Art Museum, San Francisco; British Museum, London; Cernuschi Museum, Paris; Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, Seattle; National Museum of China, Beijing; National Art Museum of China, Beijing; François-Henri Pinault Family, France; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; among others.

The traveller's boat follows the limpid waves, drifting gently upon the midstream. Frost-touched woods hold the chill of the season, while clouds and the surrounding landscape are suffused with serene tranquillity.

Pu Ru (溥儒) (1896–1963), also known as Pu Xinyu (溥心畬), was a member of the Qing Imperial family and a leading figure of the 20th century Chinese literati painting. Born into the Manchu Imperial family, he was a cousin of the last Qing Emperor, Puyi (溥儀), and received a rigorous classical education in Confucian scholarship, poetry, calligraphy, and painting, which profoundly shaped his refined artistic vision. Following the collapse of the Qing dynasty in 1911, Pu Ru dedicated himself to painting and calligraphy, earning recognition as one of the most distinguished artists of his generation. His works, often executed in the scholarly tradition, feature landscapes, birds, and figures imbued with poetic sentiment. His creation was strongly influenced by the Four Masters of the Ming dynasty and earlier literati aesthetics. Following the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949, Pu Ru relocated to Taiwan, where he continued to paint and teach. Throughout his career, his style remained deeply rooted in traditional Chinese aesthetics, characterised by expressive brushwork and a cultivated, scholarly sensibility.

See a set of four related paintings of 'Serene Landscapes,' signed Xinyu, which was sold at Sotheby's Hong Kong, 7 April 2023, lot 3106.

AN EIGHT-PANEL DOUBLE-SIDED 'COROMANDEL' LACQUER SCREEN
Cyclically dated to the Bingwu year of the Qianlong reign, corresponding to 1786 and of the period
Finely decorated on both sides, one side depicting a magnificent palace complex populated by elegant ladies and children engaged in various pursuits, with a principal hall at the centre of which a dignified lady is seated upon a throne, approached by steps guarded by a phoenix, the buildings and figures surrounded by luxuriant trees and foliage, all framed above and below by bands of archaistic mythical beasts; the reverse depicting a lotus pond with flowering lotus, auspicious plants and varied birds, including waterfowl, all framed above and below by bands of cracked-ice and foliate diaper, poetic inscription in gilt with two seals. Each panel 198cm (78in) high x 41cm (16 1/8in) wide. (8).

乾隆丙午年（1786）款彩漢宮春曉圖八開屏風 
款識：海榴初結實，菊花自芬芳。衆禽齊集合，荷底戲鴛鴦。乾隆丙午年春三月。翰林院學士顧鴻章拜賀古越李炳臣敬鎸
鈐印：顧鴻章印 李炳臣章 

The inscription on the screen may be translated as:

The pomegranate has just begun to bear fruit,
While the chrysanthemums bloom with their own fragrance.
All the birds gather together,
And mandarin ducks frolic beneath the lotus.
Spring, the third month, in the Bingwu year of the Qianlong reign.
Respectfully presented in celebration by Gu Hongzhang, Hanlin Academy Academician. Respectfully engraved by Li Bingchen of ancient Yue.

Palace scenes populated by ladies of the Court were particularly popular on Coromandel lacquer screens of the late Ming and early Qing periods. Such compositions were often based upon a frequently reproduced painting attributed to Qiu Ying (1494–1552), Spring Morning in the Han Palace. See W.De Kesel and G.Dhont, Coromandel: Lacquer Screens, Ghent, 2002, pp.48–49. The depiction of ladies engaged in cultivated pursuits, including music, painting and calligraphy, may reflect changing ideals of feminine accomplishment during this period. Compare with a twelve-leaf screen, Kangxi, illustrated in Ibid., pp.23, 31, 36.

The reverse, with a lotus pond and varied birds, likewise draws upon auspicious and literati imagery. The lotus was celebrated by the Northern Song scholar Zhou Dunyi (1017–1073) in his Ai lian shuo ('On the Love of the Lotus') as an emblem of purity and moral integrity. Birds could also carry associations with official rank, with particular species serving as insignia for the nine grades of civil officials from the Ming dynasty onwards.

Compare with a twelve-panel Coromandel lacquer screen, Kangxi, in the Art Museum, The Chinese University of Hong Kong (acc.no.2001.0660), which bears a subsequently altered Qianlong date, apparently reflecting its reuse as a birthday gift.

Heavily cast of compressed bombÃ© form, with two upright loop handles, supported on three tapered feet, with a rich golden-brown patina. 33cm (13in) wide.

The form of the present incense burner is likely inspired by one of the most classic bronze shapes produced during the Xuande period (1426-1437). These shapes in turn were drawn from the range of objects depicted in the 'Illustrations of Antiquities in the Xuanhe Hall', Xuanhe bogutu, and other antiquarian texts; while some others were modelled on fine specimens of ceramics of the Northern Song period (960-1127).

Vessels modelled after archaic shapes, such as the present example, were designated for use in the sacrificial altars located outside of the capital, at Imperial ancestral temples and within Court palaces; however, they were also presented to princely households and meritorious officials. Incense burners were also used by the literati to decorate the tables and shelves in their studio and burn fragrant incense for creating a contemplative atmosphere.

A RARE BRONZE SEAL OF GENERAL WU'AN
Dated the fifth year of the Yongli period corresponding to 1651 and of the period
Cast as a tiger seated on its haunches atop a stepped square plinth, the animal with an alert head raised upward and a tail curling to the left of the body, detailed with bulging eyes, a ruyi-shaped nose, and incised stripe markings across the body, each side of the seal top incised with an inscription, the underside cast with six characters in seal script. 9.5cm (3 3/4in) high.

南明永歷五年（1651）銅虎鈕武安將軍印 
印文：「武安將軍之印」
款識：「永歷伍年九月☐日」「禮部造」「武安將軍之印」「永字四十八號」 

The inscription on the seal face may be translated as: Seal of the General of Wu'an.

The inscriptions on the top of the seal may be translated as: Fifth year of the Yongli reign, ninth month, [day illegible]; Manufactured by the Ministry of Rites; Seal of the General Wu'an; Yong, number forty-eight.

The present seal bears exceptional historical significance as a tangible witness to the history of the Southern Ming and to the loyalty and achievement of Cao Daquan 曹大銓, General of Wu'an, who died in the resistance against the Qing dynasty.

From the inscriptions, we can tell that this seal, issued for the General of Wu'an (武安將軍, General of Military Pacification), was cast in the fifth year of the reign of the Yongli Emperor, Zhu Youlang 朱由榔 (1623-1662). In 1644, after Li Zicheng captured Beijing, the Ming dynasty lost control of northern China. The Southern Ming regime, a regional regime that continued the Ming dynasty's rule in the south, extended its activities across an extensive area in the south. Zhu Youlang, the Prince of Gui, was enthroned as Emperor in 1646 at Zhaoqing, Guangdong Province, under the support of Qu Shisi 瞿式耜 and Ding Kuichu 丁魁楚, adopting the reign title Yongli. 

The owner of the present seal is believed to be Cao Daquan. According to the Gazetteer of Guichi County (貴池縣志), Cao Daquan, courtesy name Wenlun, was a cousin of Cao Dagao. At the time, Dagao served Zhu Youlang as Grand General and held the seal of a marquis. Cao Daquan joined Dagao's camp and, in recognition of his merits, was appointed Vice-General. He was subsequently promoted to commander-in-chief and invested with the seal of the General of Wu'an. Later, he was appointed as Vice Commissioner of Surveillance for Jiangxi. In the eighth year of the Shunzhi reign (1651), he led troops out of Jiangxi to join the allied forces. While suffering from illness, Daquan was captured and taken to Zhangjiang, where he refused to submit and was put to death. 

Cao Daquan's loyalty is further commemorated in the elegy composed for him by Cao Dagao, 'A Eulogy for the Third Elder Brother, General Wu'an, Wenlun' (吊武安將軍文掄三兄), which reads: My brother's blood stained the waters of the Zhang River; in daylight, the wind carried the fragrance of his heroic spirit. Had Boyi and Shuqi likewise forsaken their integrity, the wild ferns of Shanyang would now weep in vain (吾兄頸血濺章江，白日風瓢俠骨香，假使夷齊俱喪節，空令薇蕨哭山陽). See Cao Dagao, 'Huabi lu' (化碧錄), in Ming Bieji congkan (明別集叢刊), Series 5, vol.59, Hefei, 2015, p.245.

A RARE BRONZE FIGURE OF TATHAGATA VAIROCANA
Tibet, 14th century
The deity seated in vajraparyankasana on a double-lotus base with beaded rims, his hands in bodhyagrimudra and the body clad in a diaphanous dhoti and various jewellery and a billowing scarf, the serene face with hooded eyes and sensuous lips all surmounted by an elaborate crown tied at the top with ribbons. 27cm (10 5/8in) high.

十四世紀 西藏 銅毗卢遮那佛像 

Provenance: the Burkhart collection, acquired in Zug, Switzerland, in 1998

來源： Burkhart舊藏，1998年獲得於瑞士楚格

Vairocana (Tib. rNam-par snang-mdzad), whose name may be translated as 'the Illuminator' or 'He who radiates like the sun,' is the Tathagata who presides over the centre of the cosmic mandala of the pancakula, the family of the five meditation Buddhas (dhyani Buddhas). Within this cosmological scheme Vairocana occupies the central position of the universe and, in certain mandala representations, assumes the role of the primordial Buddha, with whom he is sometimes identified; in such contexts he is referred to as Mahavairocana. His iconographic colour is white and his principal symbol is the Wheel of the Law (dharmacakra), representing the Buddha's teaching. In later depictions the wheel is sometimes shown resting within his hands.

The present large sculpture depicts Vairocana richly adorned and seated in vajraparyankasana, the full meditative posture, on a double lotus throne encircled by a beaded border. His hands are held in bodhyagrimudra, the gesture uniting skilful means (upaya) and wisdom (prajna), symbolising enlightenment and the Buddha's all-encompassing knowledge. 

Compare with a similar statue of Tathagata Vairocana, Western Tibet, 14th century, illustrated in On the Path to Enlightenment: The Berti Aschmann Foundation of Tibetan Art at the Museum Rietberg Zurich, Zurich, 1995, p.65.

Provenance: acquired in Battle, Kent, in the mid-1990s (by repute)

The present figure depicts Amitabha, the principal deity of Pure Land Buddhism and the Western Buddha among the Five Tathagatas. His name means 'immeasurable light', and he is also known as Wuliangguang (Infinite Light) and Wuliangshou (Infinite Life), reflecting his associations with longevity and pure perception. Believed to reside in Sukhavati, the Western Pure Land or 'Pure and Happy Land', Amitabha is conventionally depicted seated in meditation with the hands resting in the lap in dhyana mudra, as on the present figure. Devotion to Amitabha occupies a central place in Pure Land Buddhism, with the promise of rebirth in Sukhavati through faith and worship. As Meher McArthur notes in Reading Buddhist Art, London, 2002, p.39, the Sutra of the Pure and Happy Land teaches that mortals may attain rebirth in the Pure Land through worship of Amitabha. This salvific promise derives from the vow he made while still a bodhisattva to save all sentient beings upon attaining enlightenment.

description_block:
THE PROPERTY OF A BRITISH FAMILY è±åå®¶æèåA RARE IMPERIALLY-INSCRIBED RED AND BLACK LACQUER CARVED TEA BOWL
Qianlong seal marks and of the period, the inscription dated Bingyin year, corresponding to 1746 and of the period
The vessel with deep rounded sides rising from a straight foot, carved around the exterior through layers of cinnabar red lacquer to a black diaper-pattern ground with an Imperial poem, 'Three-Purity Tea,' Sanqing Cha, dated to the Bingyin year (corresponding to 1746) followed by the seals Qian and Long, all between two borders of ruyi and lotus petal designs encircling the rim and foot, with leiwen band around the foot, the interior lacquered brownish-red. 11.2cm (4 7/8in) diam.

清乾隆丙寅年（1746） 御製剔紅御題詩三清茶盌
印：「乾」、「隆」 

Provenance: Sir George Mowlem Burt KBE (1884–1964), Surrey, and thence by descent

來源：大英帝國爵級司令勛章獲得者George Mowlem Burt爵士（1884-1964），英國薩裏，并由後人保存迄今 

Born in Westminster on 10 January 1884, Sir George Mowlem Burt KBE joined the family firm, John Mowlem & Co., in 1902, following in the footsteps of his father and uncle. He subsequently became supervising director of the company and was involved in a number of major engineering and building projects. He was a prominent figure in the development of the civil engineering industry, serving as a founding member of the Federation of Civil Engineering Contractors and on various Government committees and missions. He was also Master of the Worshipful Company of Paviors. Outside his professional life, Burt was a distinguished fencer, winning the British épée championship in 1922 and representing Great Britain in épée at the 1920 Olympic Games. He was knighted in 1942 and died at Blindley Heath, Surrey, on 1 September 1964. An enthusiastic collector of art, his collection included paintings, ivory, netsuke and jade.

The present bowl was almost certainly intended for use as part of an Imperial tea service associated with the Qianlong Emperor's New Year tea gatherings. It is carved with the Emperor's celebrated poem Sanqing cha ('Three Purities Tea'), composed in the Bingyin year (1746), when he marked his thirty-sixth birthday by drinking tea in his Guyue Studio during the depths of winter. 

The inscription reads:

梅花色不妖，佛手香且潔。松實味芳腴，三品殊清絕。烹以折腳鐺，沃之承筐雪。火候辨魚蟹，鼎煙迭生滅。越甌潑仙乳，氈廬適禪悅。五蘊淨大半，可悟不可說。馥馥兜羅遞，活活雲漿澈。偓佺遺可餐，林逋賞時別。懶舉趙州案，頗笑玉川譎。寒宵聽行漏，古月看懸玦。軟飽趁幾餘，敲吟興無竭。乾隆丙寅小春御題 

Which may be translated as:

The plum blossom in appearance not ostentatious,
The finger citron, scented and fresh,
Pine nuts of most fragrant aroma,
Three ingredients of outstanding purity.
An infusion is brewed in a shallow tripod vessel,
And the ingredients steeped in snow-water collected in a bamboo casket.
After coming to a boil, bubbles like the eyes of fish or crabs can be seen in the surface of the water,
Steam rises from the tripod appearing to alternate between Utpadanirodha birth and death.
Teacups from the kilns of Yue sprinkled with Immortals' milk,
The warmth of my yurt is agreeable to the joy of the mystic trance.
The five Buddhist Skanda purify the greater part of all things,
Spiritual awakening may occur but cannot be spoken of.
The sweet smelling ingredients are dealt with and suitably delivered,
Silky smooth the Immortals' wine, clear and limpid.
Wo Quan's offering may be eaten.
Lin Bu can admire the change of seasons.
Nonchalantly the Koan of the Zhaozhou monk may be uttered,
And the eccentricity of Yu Chuanzi laughed at heartily.
On a cold night in winter, listening to the sound of the water clock,
From the Guyue Studio I observe the moon, hanging in the sky like a jade archer's ring.
I take advantage of what remains to drink my fill,
And chant deliberately so that I might arise without exhaustion.
Composed by the Emperor in the tenth lunar month of the Bingyin year [corresponding to 1746] during the reign of the Qianlong Emperor.

The poem celebrates a distinctive infusion prepared from plum blossom, finger citron and pine kernels, ingredients presented to the Emperor during a visit to the sacred Buddhist mountain of Wutai. Brewed with freshly collected snow water, these three components were believed to produce a tea of exceptional fragrance and purity. Beyond describing its preparation, the poem reflects on the moral and spiritual qualities associated with tea, drawing parallels with Buddhist ideals of purity, restraint and simplicity.

A discerning patron of both the arts and tea culture, the Qianlong Emperor frequently combined the appreciation of works of art with refined tea drinking in intimate palace gatherings. Tea was prepared and served in carefully selected vessels drawn from the Imperial collection, which included celebrated ceramics and utensils spanning many centuries. Conversation is said to have ranged from the antiquity and glaze of individual tea wares to the qualities of particular tea leaves, while guests judged each infusion by its colour, fragrance and flavour.

During the New Year celebrations, the Emperor customarily hosted a tea banquet in the Palace of Cherished Glory (Chonghua Gong) within the Forbidden City. Invited officials were encouraged to compose poetry, and those whose verses most impressed the Emperor were rewarded with a Sanqing cha tea bowl such as the present example, making these vessels tangible expressions of Imperial literary culture as well as objects of refined craftsmanship. 

The poem is preserved in the Qing Gaozong yuzhi shiwen quanji (Complete Collection of the Qianlong Emperor's Imperial Poems and Prose), Yuzhi shiwen chuji, vol.1, juan 36, p.17. It contains numerous literary and Buddhist allusions, reflecting the Emperor's wide-ranging intellectual interests. Although the Qing Court was closely associated with Tibetan Buddhism, many of the poem's references derive from the vocabulary and traditions of Chan Buddhism, in keeping with established Chinese literary conventions.

Among the figures invoked is the legendary mountain recluse Wo Quan, famed for subsisting on pine nuts and reputedly offering them to the sage Emperor Yao. According to tradition, Yao declined the gift and thereby forfeited their life-extending properties; the Qianlong Emperor humorously suggests that he himself would have accepted them without hesitation.

The poem also alludes to the celebrated Chan master Zhaozhou Congshen (778–897). One of the best-known koans associated with the monk recounts how every visitor, regardless of circumstance, was simply invited to 'drink tea', illustrating the Chan emphasis on direct experience rather than abstract explanation. By referencing this episode, the Emperor subtly likens his own tea gatherings to occasions of cultivated fellowship and enlightened discourse.

Comparable examples include a similar carved lacquer bowl with the same poem, Qianlong seal mark and of the period, in the Palace Museum, Beijing, illustrated in The Emperor's Private Paradise: Treasures from the Forbidden City, New Haven, 2011, no.57. Another example from the Beijing Antique Company Collection is illustrated in Gems of Beijing Cultural Relics Series: Works of Decorative Arts I, Beijing, 2006, pl. 25.
