Elephants occupied a prominent place in the Chinese auspicious repertoire, where they were admired both for their imposing physical presence and for the favourable associations of their name. The character for elephant, xiang (象), is a homophone for xiang (祥), meaning 'auspicious' or 'propitious', making the animal a popular emblem of good fortune. In art of the Ming and Qing dynasties, elephants frequently appear in conjunction with boys (tongzi), whose presence alludes to wishes for numerous descendants and the continuation of the family line. The flowering spray carried by the boy in the present carving, likely representing peony, further enriches this auspicious programme. Celebrated as the 'King of Flowers', the peony symbolises wealth, honour and high rank, and its combination with the elephant may therefore be interpreted as a wish for prosperity, distinction and enduring good fortune.

Beyond their symbolic significance, elephants occupied an important place within the ceremonial life of the Qing Court. Live elephants were maintained by the Imperial Household and regularly appeared in state processions and ritual occasions, where their impressive size and exotic origins enhanced the grandeur of Imperial spectacle. Many were presented as tribute from the southern frontiers of the empire and from kingdoms of Southeast Asia, including Siam, Burma and other tributary states. Contemporary paintings show elephants participating in major Court ceremonies in Beijing, while the Imperial Elephant Stable (Xiangfang) was situated near Xuanwumen, where the animals were housed and trained under official supervision. Their presence at Court served not only as a display of Imperial magnificence but also as a tangible demonstration of the far-reaching influence of the Qing empire, lending additional resonance to artistic representations such as the present lot. See Copy of the Kangxi Emperor's Sixtieth Birthday Celebration, scroll one, late 18th century, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated by E.Rawski and J.Rawson, China: The Three Emperors 1662-1795, London, 2005, p.101, no.24.

See a related white and russet jade carving of an elephant with a man standing by a boy, Qing dynasty, in the Qing Court Collection, The Complete Collection of Treasures of the Palace Museum: Jadeware (III), Hong Kong, 1995, p.117, no.97. 

Compare with a related white and russet jade 'elephant and foreigner' group, 18th century, which was sold at Sotheby's Hong Kong, 9 April 2024, lot 3702. See also a smaller white jade carving of an elephant with boys, Qianlong, which was sold at Christie's London, 14 May 2013, lot 81, and a creamy white jade figure of an elephant and boy, Qing dynasty, which was sold at Christie's New York, 25 March 2022, lot 1260.

The elephant was among the most auspicious animals in the Chinese decorative repertoire. The standing attendant depicted beside the animal appears to represent a foreigner, identifiable by his distinctive hooded cloak and staff. He subsequently became supervising director of the company and was involved in a number of major engineering and building projects. He was a prominent figure in the development of the civil engineering industry, serving as a founding member of the Federation of Civil Engineering Contractors and on various Government committees and missions. He was also Master of the Worshipful Company of Paviors. Outside his professional life, Burt was a distinguished fencer, winning the British épée championship in 1922 and representing Great Britain in épée at the 1920 Olympic Games. He was knighted in 1942 and died at Blindley Heath, Surrey, on 1 September 1964. An enthusiastic collector of art, his collection included paintings, ivory, netsuke and jade.

The present incense burner and cover would have formed part of a three-piece garniture comprising an incense burner, a vase and an incense box, often referred to as the 'Three Accessories' or sanshi. See two examples of such sets in spinach-green jade in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in Compendium of Collections in the Palace Museum: Jade 10 Qing Dynasty, Beijing, 2011, no.111, and another in the Musée des Arts Décoratifs, Paris, illustrated by Tsao Huei-chung, Jade: From Emperors to Art Déco, Paris, 2016, no.132. Such sets were placed on the scholar's table in the Qing Court for the burning of incense.

The form derives from the archaic bronze tradition, in line with the Qing Imperial project of 'restoring ancient ways', which conceived of antiquity as embodying qualities of sincerity, simplicity and restrained vitality. The Qianlong Emperor in particular favoured the adaptation of archaic forms into contemporary designs, commissioning the systematic study of antiquities through compilations such as the Catalogue of Xiqing Antiquities (Xi Qing Gu Jian), which were made available to Court craftsmen as models for inspiration. See Chang Li-tuan, The Refined Taste of the Emperor: Special Exhibition of Archaic and Pictorial Jades of the Ch'ing Court, Taipei, 1997, pp.49–50.

A related archaic bronze vessel is illustrated by Wang Tao, Chinese Bronzes from the Meiyintang Collection, London, 2009, no.127, where the author notes that the unusual form suggests a function distinct from conventional ritual food vessels and proposes that it may instead have served as a pigment container. It is also notable that vessels of this type were produced in jade during the late Shang to early Western Zhou periods. See Prof Ch'eng Te-k'un, 'The T'u-lu Colour-Container of the Shang-Chou Period', Bulletin of the Museum of Far Eastern Antiquities, 1965, vol.37, pp.239–50.

Compare also a similar spinach-green jade tulu and cover, late 18th century, in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, illustrated by M.Wilson, Chinese Jades, London, 2004, pl.52.

See a related spinach-green jade incense burner and cover, tulu, Qianlong, which was sold at Bonhams London, 12 May 2022, lot 115.

A PAIR OF EXCEPTIONALLY RARE 'TANG YING' FAMILLE ROSE TEA CADDIES
Qianlong
Each of square shape, the front and reverse faces variously painted with leafy floral branches, including peach blossom, poppy, musk mallow, and camellia, each accompanied by seals and poetic inscriptions, the sides finely enamelled with foliate and floral scrolls reserved on yellow and red diaper grounds respectively, the necks and bases unglazed, two later fitted wood covers. Each 16.8cm (6 5/8in) high. (4).

清乾隆 粉彩詩文花卉四方茶葉罐一對 
款識及鈐印：好是九重春色醉，莫隨三汲浪花肥。「陶」「鑄」
最愛清香可蠲忿，時時風送入窗紗。「陶」「鑄」
清似臘梅梅太早，色如金菊菊猶遲。「幽窗」
群芳散盡羨山花，肯共松篁傲歲華。「翰」「墨」

Provenance: a British private collection
Toovey's, Pulborough, 23 February 2017, lot 1130

來源： 英國私人收藏 
Toovey's拍賣行，英國普爾伯勒，2017年2月23日，拍品編號1130

The present lot represents an exceptional fusion of the refined aesthetic sensibilities of the Qing Court and literati tradition with the exquisite craftsmanship of the Imperial Kiln in Jingdezhen. It reflects the artistic vision of Tang Ying (1682-1756), the Superintendent of the Imperial Kilns, as well as the collaborative nature of production at the Imperial kilns. 

It constitutes a harmonious fourfold integration of poetry, calligraphy, painting and seal (詩書畫印), which is a defining characteristic of traditional Chinese literati painting. The tea caddies bear the seals taozhu (陶鑄 making pottery and casting metal), youchuang (幽窗 the secluded window) and hanmo (翰墨 brushes and ink). According to Huang Qinghua's research, the taozhu and hanmo seals are leisure seals associated with the works of Lü Ji (呂績). It is possible that the painting and calligraphy on the tea caddies may be attributed to Lü Ji. He was a highly valued Imperial kiln painter working under the celebrated superintendent of the Imperial porcelain kilns, Tang Ying (1683-1756). He specialised in overglaze painting of flowers, birds, and landscapes, and was highly accomplished in all four major styles of Chinese calligraphy, with running script being his particular strength. He began working at the Imperial kiln factory after the seventh year of the Qianlong reign (1742), entering Tang Ying's circle of artisans and serving the Imperial kilns for more than twenty years. At the time, the finest Imperial porcelains commissioned by Tang Ying and decorated with poetry, inscriptions, and other literary compositions were mostly produced by Lü Ji's hand.

The inscriptions are elegantly executed in running script and clerical scripts, and may be translated as:

Better to be drunk on the spring colours; than to follow the swelling waves that promise glory.
Dearest of all is the pure fragrance that dispels resentment; again and again, the breeze bears it through the gauze of my window.
As pure as the wax plum, yet the plum blooms too early; as golden as the chrysanthemum, yet the chrysanthemum blooms too late.
When all the flowers have faded, I envy the mountain bloom; Would it, like pine and bamboo, stand proud through the years?

The front and reverse faces of the tea caddies are exquisitely painted in famille rose with flowering branches of peach blossom, poppy, musk mallow, and camellia, representing the four seasons. In depicting flowers of diverse forms and colours, the artist makes masterful use of an extensive range of pastel tones, carefully modulating variations in shade and the density of the brushwork with remarkable precision. The floral compositions reflect the characteristic style of Qing Court flower-and-bird painting as well as the exceptional technical accomplishments of the craftsmen at Jingdezhen. 

It was common practice for decorative motifs produced at the Qing Imperial kilns to be designed initially by Court painters. Following Imperial approval, the designs were transmitted to Jingdezhen, where skilled craftsmen reproduced them on porcelain according to the original models. As seen in the present lot, the Qing Court bird-and-flower tradition drew inspiration from earlier masters, notably Yun Shouping 惲壽平 (1633-1690), who invented the 'boneless' style. See ten album leaves entitled Flowers and Plants by Yun Shouping, in the Qing Court Collection, the Palace Museum, Beijing, illustrated in China: The Three Emperors 1662-1795, London, 2005, p.330-331. This work could also reflect the influence of Jiang Tingxi 蔣廷錫 and Zou Yigui 鄒一桂 who are likewise regarded as important practitioners who brought Yun Shouping's style into the Imperial Court. See Album of Flowers by Zou Yigui, dated 1734, in the Qing Court Collection, the Palace Museum, Taipei, illustrated in Harmony and Integrity: The Yongzheng Emperor and His Times (雍正：清世宗文物大展), Taipei, 2000, pp.300-302. See also a pair of famille rose 'poppy' bowls, decorated with flowers closely comparable to the poppies depicted on the present lot, Yongzheng six-character marks and of the period, which was sold at Christie's Hong Kong, 29 November 2017, lot 2806. 

The decoration on the sides of the tea caddies notably echoes the style described in the Qing Imperial archives as yangcai (洋彩, literally meaning 'Western colours'). Yangcai wares ranked among the most prestigious products of the Imperial Kiln Factory at Jingdezhen and were principally made for display and use within a small number of important palaces at the Qing Court. According to Liao Baoxiu's research, yangcai employed the same enamel pigments as falangcai porcelain. However, because it adopted Western decorative motifs, techniques and painting methods that differed from traditional Chinese painting, it came to be known as yangcai. 

The floral motifs depicted on the sides of the present lot should be 'western lotus' (xifan lian 西番蓮), a general term for flowers introduced from foreign regions and so named because their petals resemble those of the lotus. In addition, the arrangement of floral motifs on a red diaper ground on one of the tea caddies corresponds with the decorative technique of 'adding flowers to brocade' (jinshang tianhua 錦上添花). Invented by Tang Ying, this technique became a main feature of yangcai wares of the Qianlong reign. See a yangcai landscape vase with comparable floral motifs on red diaper ground, Qianlong mark and of the period, in the Qing Court Collection, the Palace Museum, Beijing, illustrated in The Complete Collection of the Treasures of the Palace Museum: Porcelains with Cloisonne Enamel Decoration and Famille Rose Decoration (故宮博物館藏文物珍品大系：琺琅彩·粉彩), Hong Kong, 1999, pl.114. 

Yangcai wares, like falangcai wares, were principally displayed in the Palace of Heavenly Purity (乾清宮 Qianqinggong) and the Hall of Mental Cultivation (養心殿 Yangxindian), and the Old Summer Palace (圓明園 Yuanmingyuan). Apart from those, they were rarely displayed in other palace buildings. Given their rarity and prestige at the time of production, such objects were not commonly encountered even within the Qing Imperial palace, let alone beyond its walls. For further discussion, see Liao Baoxiu, 'Adding Flowers to Brocade: a Discussion of Yangcai' (錦上添花話洋彩), in The Palace Museum Research Monthly (故宮文物月刊), 2006, vol.280, pp.4-23. 

As the superintendent of the Imperial Kilns, Tang Ying played a significant role in the development of yangcai technique at the Imperial Kilns. According to the Qianlong Period Record Archives (乾隆記事檔), in the tenth month of the second year of the Qianlong reign (1737), the Emperor was highly pleased with the yellow-ground yangcai palace bowls decorated with western-style flowers and instructed Tang Ying to adopt their decoration for porcelain boxes and vases. Compare the yellow ground sides of one of the tea caddies with a square vase with comparable western floral decoration on a yellow ground in yangcai painted enamels, Qianlong, in the Qing Court Collection, the Palace Museum, Taipei (acc.no.故瓷005104N000000000).

The Qianlong Emperor was an avid tea drinker and also cultivated the refined literati tradition of tea appreciation. Following his first Southern Tour in the sixteenth year of the Qianlong reign (1751), he was deeply influenced by the cultural and scenic environment of Jiangnan. Thereafter, he established dedicated tea pavilions within his various Imperial residences for the practice of tea appreciation, and composed many poems on the subject of tea. His appreciation of tea naturally extended to a discerning regard for the vessels used in its preparation and enjoyment. 

During the Qing dynasty, the presentation of gifts by local officials to the Emperor was a formalised practice. It served not only as a means for officials to demonstrate their loyalty to the sovereign and cultivate personal relationships, but also as an integral part of Qing Court administration and official culture. Against this background, the present lot, a unique example, was probably made upon a specific order by Tang Ying at the Imperial Kilns and presented to the Qianlong Emperor as a gift. See a rectangular tea caddy of the same shape as the present lot, depicted in Court Version of 'Spring Dawn in the Han Palace' (院本漢宮春曉圖), by the Court painters Sun Hu, Zhou Kun and Ding Guanpeng, dated to the sixth year of the Qianlong period (1741), illustrated in Empty Vessels, Replenished Minds: The Culture, Practice, and Art of Tea (也可以清心：茶器·茶事·茶畫), Taipei, 2002, p.145, no.123. 

See an imitation marble glaze tea caddy of the same shape and similarly characterised by an unglazed base and neck, with two seals reading tao and jun, dated as probably Yongzheng reign, in the collection of the Museums Scotland, Edinburgh (acc.no.A.1929.81).

A RARE GUAN-TYPE 'SASH-TIED' VASE
Yongzheng
The body of compressed globular form moulded with concave grooves, rising from a short, straight foot through rounded shoulders to a waisted neck terminating in an everted rim, the shoulders applied with a sash tied in a bow, covered overall in a thick, opaque greyish-blue glaze suffused with a network of fine beige crackles, the unglazed foot rim dressed in a dark brown slip. 20cm (7 7/8in) high.

清雍正 仿官釉包袱式瓶 

Provenance: Henry Potter Stevens (1875-1965), England

來源：Henry Potter Stevens (1875-1965)，英格蘭

Henry Potter Stevens (1875–1965) was born in London and studied at Oxford University and Heidelberg University before establishing a distinguished career as a chemist in the rubber industry. He was a talented artist whose works were exhibited at the Royal Academy, Grosvenor Gallery, Redfern Gallery, and the Royal Institute of Painters, among other prominent institutions. Stevens was also a collector and expert on Chinese and Japanese art, acquiring many works from Glendining & Co., Sotheby's, and Christie's. His collection of Japanese inrō was sold at Bonhams in 2012.

The present lot is made in reminiscence of the Song dynasty Guan wares. Song dynasty Guan kiln porcelain is distinguished by its restrained forms and an exceptionally fine, smooth, jade-like glaze, embodying an aesthetic of natural simplicity and unpretentious elegance. Reproductions of Guan kiln wares were undertaken primarily by the Imperial kilns, where considerable resources were devoted to capturing both the form and spirit of the Song originals. The most accomplished examples date to the Yongzheng and Qianlong reigns of the Qing dynasty, as exemplified by the present lot.

The form of the present lot carries an auspicious connotation, as the term 'wrapping cloth' (包袱 baofu) is homophonous with 包福 (baofu), meaning 'to wrap up good fortune,' thereby imbuing the vessel with the symbolic wish for the gathering and preservation of blessings.

See a similar Guan-type 'sash-tied' vase, Yongzheng seal mark and of the period, in the Qing Court Collection, Palace Museum, Beijing, illustrated in Qing Dynasty Imperial Kiln Porcelain in the Collection of the Palace Museum (故宮博物院藏清代御窯瓷器), vol.1 (Part 2), Beijing, 2005, pp.54-55.

See a related Guan-type vase, Yongzheng period, which was sold at Sotheby's London, 15 May 2013, lot 229.

Jeremy Mason is a noted bibliophile and a retired dealer in Chinese and Japanese art who started his career at Christie's in the late 1960s, particularly known for his collection of Oscar Wilde books and ephemera, sold at Bonhams London in February 2026. 

The present vase is a particularly rare example of Qianlong period Beijing Imperial painted enamel, notable for its Imperial yellow ground and the exceptionally restrained yet complex arrangement of its decoration. The combination of bold floral motifs, carefully controlled palette and expansive areas of yellow ground appears to be distinctive among surviving examples, giving the vase a strong sense of visual clarity and refinement.

The Imperial workshops for painted enamel were established in Beijing during the Kangxi reign, following the introduction of European enamel-painting techniques to the Qing Court through Jesuits. Early Kangxi examples are characterised by relatively bold compositions, strong contrasts of colour and a limited but vivid palette, often set against yellow grounds. See for example a painted enamel vase with peony designs on yellow-ground shaped panel, Kangxi four-character mark and of the period, in the Qing Court Collection at the Palace Museum, Beijing, illustrated in Compendium of Collections in the Palace Museum: Enamels, vol.5, Beijing, 2011, p.32, no.5. See also a painted enamel flower basket with peony design, Kangxi four character mark and of the period, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in Ibid., no.30. The present vase may be understood in this context, harking back to the boldness, simplicity of composition and concentrated palette of early Kangxi painted enamels, while demonstrating the greater technical refinement achieved by the Qianlong period.

By the Qianlong reign, Beijing painted enamel had developed into a highly sophisticated Imperial art form, with increasingly precise brushwork, subtle modelling and more elaborate decorative schemes. Nevertheless, the present vase deliberately eschews the densely worked compositions frequently encountered on Qianlong period painted enamels, instead retaining the directness and visual strength associated with the earlier Kangxi tradition. See for example, a circular painted enamel box and cover with lotus on yellow ground, Qianlong four-character mark and of the period, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in Ibid., no.89. See also two yellow-ground painted enamel teapots and covers, Qianlong four-character marks and of the period, in the Qing Court Collection, illustrated in Ibid., nos.106-107. Compare the mark with a similar one on a painted enamel 'crackled ice and plum blossom' vase, Qianlong four-character mark and of the period, illustrated in Ibid., no.62.

The peony was among the most auspicious flowers in the Chinese decorative tradition, symbolising wealth, honour and prosperity and commonly known as the fugui hua (富貴花), the 'flower of wealth and honour'. Its luxuriant form and sumptuous blossoms also made it particularly appropriate to Imperial decoration. On the present vase, the peony is rendered in a manner that combines the auspicious symbolism of the flower with the highly controlled aesthetic of Imperial painted enamel, resulting in a decoration that is both visually restrained and rich in meaning.

The inscription on the lapis lazuli boulder may be translated as:

An Imperial poem. Your fragrance rises above the dust of the ordinary, your graceful bearing is of a lofty character. You take your place among a grove of gentlemen; how could you ever disdain a stranger newly arrived?

The inscription is taken from a poem by the Qianlong Emperor entitled 戲成四友圖各題以句 ('Amusingly composing verses for a painting of the Four Friends'), specifically the verse on the orchid, and is recorded in 御製詩三集 (Imperial Poems, Third Collection), juan 2, composed in the twenty-fifth year of the Qianlong reign (1760). The four poems celebrate the pine, bamboo, plum and orchid, collectively known as the 'Four Friends'. In the present verse, the orchid is personified as a cultivated gentleman, its fragrance and elegant bearing symbolising moral refinement, purity and lofty character.

In the Qing Court, potted miniature landscapes and floral displays formed an important part of interior decoration and were frequently fashioned from prized materials, contributing to the sumptuous environment of the Imperial palaces. Particularly in northern China, where the seasons were clearly differentiated, such permanent representations of flowers, plants and landscapes provided an enduring alternative to living specimens.

The potted miniature landscapes preserved in the Qing Court Collection were produced by the Imperial Workshops, as well as being presented as tribute from the provinces or offered by nobles and high-ranking officials. Their varied materials and techniques consequently reflect different regional traditions. The present lot is most likely to have been produced in Guangzhou, where painted enamel was particularly favoured for jardinières used in miniature landscapes. The gilded treatment of the trunks and branches, as seen on the present lot, is also characteristic of such Guangzhou-made arrangements.

Sir Harry M. Garner KBE CB (1891-1977) was a distinguished mathematician who joined the Royal Aircraft Establishment in 1927. He served as Director of Scientific Research at the Ministry of Aircraft Production in 1943 and Chief Scientist at the Ministry of Supply between 1949 and 1953. As an eminent collector and scholar of East Asian art, Garner published extensively on Chinese decorative arts, producing authoritative reference works on blue and white porcelain, lacquer, and cloisonné enamels. Together with Lady Garner, he assembled one of the finest private collections of Oriental art in Britain, much of which was later donated to the British Museum, London, and the Victoria and Albert Museum, London. Garner was deeply involved with the Oriental Ceramic Society, serving as Honorary Secretary from 1951 to 1967 and as President from 1967 to 1971. 

The Imperial Enamel Workshops in Beijing were established during the Kangxi reign, producing painted enamel wares for the Qing Court in a highly specialised and technically demanding medium. Kangxi period painted enamels are now well represented in major museum collections, whereas surviving examples from the Yongzheng reign are considerably rarer. Yongzheng period Beijing enamel is consequently of particular importance for the study of the development of the medium at the Qing Court. As seen in the present lot, wares produced during the Yongzheng period were predominantly small in size, characterised by well-proportioned forms and refined painting. See a related oval box and cover, Yongzheng four-character mark, decorated with flowers, in the Qing Court Collection at the Palace Museum, Taipei, illustrated in A Garland of Treasures: Masterpieces of Precious Crafts in the Museum Collection, Taipei, 2014, p.44.

The present box and cover is a fine example of Beijing enamel of the Yongzheng period. According to archival records, during the Kangxi and Yongzheng periods, Imperial painted enamel wares were manufactured predominantly at the Palace and princely workshops in the capital. It was not until the thirteenth year of the Qianlong reign (1748) that the Qing Court first instructed officials in Guangdong to commission painted enamel wares as Imperial tribute wares. Thereafter, production patterns gradually shifted.

The unusual form of the present box appears to derive from the Japanese musubibumi (結び文), a stylised form representing a letter folded and tied into a knot, which was employed in Japanese decorative arts from at least the 17th century, particularly in the production of small lacquer and ceramic containers. An early example is a polychrome musubibumi-form incense container by Nonomura Ninsei, 17th century, in the Osaka Museum of Oriental Ceramics (acc.no.02593). The adoption of this distinctly Japanese form in Yongzheng period painted enamel is especially noteworthy in view of the Emperor's well known appreciation of Japanese lacquer. An 18th century black and gilt lacquer knot-shaped box and cover in the Qing Court Collection at the Palace Museum, Taipei (acc. no. 故漆000485N000000000), possibly of Japanese manufacture, provides a further interesting comparison.

At the same time, the form would have acquired an auspicious resonance within the Chinese context: the character for 'knot' (jie 結) is a near homophone of ji (吉), meaning 'auspiciousness' or 'good fortune'. The present box may therefore represent a Japanese-derived form adapted for the Qing Court and invested with auspicious meaning within the Chinese decorative tradition. The butterfly motif is another prominent feature of the design. The word for butterfly (hu 蝴) forms part of a homophone for fu (福), meaning 'blessing' or 'good fortune'. Furthermore, as butterflies are frequently depicted in pairs, they have long been associated with happiness, conjugal harmony, and the flourishing of descendants. Together, these motifs convey a layered message of auspiciousness, prosperity, and familial felicity.

See a related Beijing enamel yellow-ground 'peaches' seal paste box and cover, Yongzheng four-character mark and of the period, which was sold at Sotheby's Hong Kong, 7 October 2015, lot 3783.

The colour of the present vase is known in Chinese as niehuang (涅黃), literally 'opaque yellow'. The term nie (涅) is believed to derive from the Manchu word dushun meaning 'dim' or 'opaque', a reference to the distinctive opacity of the material. This colour was achieved through the addition of an opacifying agent to the glass body, producing a rich, opaque yellow appearance.

The taotie mask adorning the present lot derives from the taotie motif found on archaic bronze vessels. Reflecting the Qianlong Emperor's profound reverence for antiquity, Qing Court craftsmen frequently drew inspiration from ancient prototypes, reinterpreting their forms and decorative motifs in a wide range of media as seen in the present lot. Compare with a related yellow glass 'taotie' brush washer, Qianlong, in the collection of the Beijing Palace Museum, illustrated in Chunshuiqiuying: gugong bowuyuan cang Qingdai boliqi (春水秋英：故宮博物院藏清代玻璃器), Beijing, 2009, pp.168-169.

Peter Hariolf Plesch (1918-2013) was a Professor of Chemistry at Keele University and a dedicated collector of Chinese art, particularly ceramics and glass. Born in Frankfurt, he moved to the UK in 1933 with his father, Janos Plesch, a close associate of Albert Einstein. Educated at Harrow and Cambridge, Plesch became known for his exceptional collection of Chinese glass. After retiring, he and his wife moved to an Art Deco-influenced house in Newcastle-under-Lyme, where they created a private museum for their Chinese and Korean art. Known for his meticulous attention to detail, Plesch kept thorough records of expert opinions on his collection. The present lot is a rare example of a Tibetan Buddhist ga'u, or portable reliquary shrine. Worn by monks and lay devotees or placed within a domestic shrine, ga'u boxes were designed to house sacred contents such as miniature images, relics, manuscripts, or consecrated substances, which were believed to confer spiritual protection and blessings upon the owner. The distinctive arched form of the present example follows traditional Tibetan portable shrines, while its surface is richly ornamented with various auspicious Buddhist symbols appropriate for its sacred function. 

This iconographic programme reflects the close artistic and religious exchanges between the Ming Court and Tibetan Buddhist institutions, during which cloisonné enamelling was successfully adapted to forms associated with Tibetan Buddhist ritual practice. See a related cloisonné enamel box and cover decorated with the Eight Buddhist Emblems, Jingtai mark, in the Uldry Collection, illustrated by H.Brinker and A.Lutz, Chinesisches Cloisonné: Die Sammlung Pierre Uldry, Zürich, 1985, no.79.

Jade belt plaques, known from as early as the Northern Zhou period, remained highly fashionable through to the Ming dynasty. In Buddhist iconography, Guanyin is frequently depicted flanked by Shancai (善財) and Longnü (龍女), as exemplified in the present lot, symbolizing her role as a compassionate guide leading all beings toward enlightenment. The earliest known visual representation of Guanyin accompanied by both Shancai and Longnü dates to the 12th century, including a wall painting of the Water-Moon Guanyin with two attendants in the Yulin Caves, Western Xia dynasty (1038–1227), illustrated in Yulin ku (榆林窟), Nanjing, 2019, pp.139–140. The emergence of this triadic imagery—likely originating in Zhejiang—reflects the deep interconnection between The Mahavaipulya Sutra (華嚴經), which recounts the legend of Shancai, and the Lotus Sutra (蓮華經), which references Longnü. During the Ming dynasty, the rise of vernacular literature and storytelling, particularly The Complete Biography of Guanyin of the Southern Sea (南海觀音全傳), further enriched and popularised the narrative of Guanyin's association with Shancai and Longnü, solidifying this imagery in Buddhist art. For more discussion on the iconography of Guanyin accompanied by Shancai and Longnü, see Chen Junji, 'Guanyin pusa xieshi juanshu zhong de shancai yu longnü zuhe' (觀音菩薩脅侍眷屬中的善財與龍女組合), The Palace Museum Monthly of Chinese Art, Taipei, 2022(473), pp.98-109.

Provenance: William Clayton Ltd., London

The present powerful carving depicts a scholar standing beside a large plantain leaf, upon which he practises calligraphy. Such imagery belongs to the rich visual language of the Chinese literati tradition, where the cultivation of brushwork was regarded not merely as an artistic exercise, but as a form of moral and spiritual self-cultivation. The scene may also allude to the celebrated Tang dynasty monk-calligrapher Huaisu (737–799), who, according to tradition, planted banana trees around his temple and used their leaves as a writing surface when he could not afford sufficient paper for practice.

Plantain leaves (bajiao 芭蕉) held layered associations in Chinese painting, poetry and Buddhist thought. Their broad surfaces resemble sheets of paper, and historical sources suggest that impoverished scholars occasionally used the leaves as temporary writing surfaces when paper was scarce. As a result, the motif came to symbolise scholarly diligence, humility, and perseverance in study. Even the Qianlong Emperor, who certainly did not lack access to fine paper, when a prince, had himself depicted as a scholar practicing calligraphy on a plantain leaf to show his humble diligence; see Prince Hongli Practicing Calligraphy on a Banana Leaf, c.1730, in the Palace Museum, Beijing, illustrated by E.Rawski and J.Rawson, China: The Three Emperors 1662-1795, London, 2005, p.277, no.187. 

Beyond this practical association, the plantain possessed profound poetic and philosophical resonance. In Chinese literature, the sound of rain falling upon banana leaves became a celebrated image of solitude, introspection and the passing of time. The leaves themselves, which unfurl gradually before tearing easily in wind and rain, suggested both the unfolding of wisdom and the fragility of worldly ambition.

The motif also carried Buddhist connotations. In Buddhist texts, the banana plant was frequently employed as a metaphor for impermanence and emptiness, since its trunk possesses no solid core but consists only of layered sheaths. Within this context, the image of a scholar writing upon a plantain leaf may be understood as a meditation upon the transient nature of fame, examination success and human endeavour itself.

The reverse is carved with a deer gazing upward at a flying crane, a rebus associated with longevity, high rank and harmonious retirement from official life. The pairing recalls decorative motifs seen on Kangxi period blue and white porcelain. The close stylistic and iconographic parallels with these late 17th and early 18th century decorative arts provide a persuasive point of comparison for dating the present carving. See for example, a blue and white crane, pine and deer, phoenix-tail vase, Kangxi, illustrated in Qing Shunzhi Kangxi chao qinghua ci, Beijing, 2005, pp.476-477, no.307.

Compare with a related large pale greyish-green and russet jade mountain, 17th/18th century, with scholars, which was sold at Christie's New York, 14 September 2012, lot 1019.

The Palmer family were the founders of Huntley & Palmers, the Reading biscuit manufacturers, and assembled an important collection of Chinese art. The collection was begun by William Howard Palmer (1865–1923) and his wife Ada (1870–1953) at their home, Heathlands, near Wokingham, and passed to their only son, Reginald Howard Reed Palmer (1898–1970). Reginald and his wife Lena (1900–1981) subsequently added the greatest number of pieces to the collection, acquiring extensively from leading London dealers including John Sparks, Bluett & Sons, H.R.N. Norton, Spink & Son and Mallett. Reginald was an early member of the Oriental Ceramics Society, and the collection was widely exhibited and published, including in the Oriental Ceramics Society's exhibitions of Chinese Jades in 1948 and Enamelled Polychrome Porcelain of the Manchu Dynasty in 1951, and the Ashmolean Museum's exhibition of Chinese Painted Enamels in 1978.

The present lot depicts Chang'e (嫦娥), the Chinese goddess of the Moon, holding the Jade Rabbit (玉兔), one of the most enduring figures in Chinese mythology. According to legend, Chang'e attained Immortality after consuming the elixir of life and ascended to the Moon, where she resides in the Moon Palace. Accompanying her is the Jade Rabbit, her faithful companion, who is traditionally shown pounding the ingredients for the elixir of Immortality with a mortar and pestle. Together, Chang'e and the Jade Rabbit became powerful symbols of the Moon, Immortality, and longevity, particularly celebrated during the Mid-Autumn Festival. Their appearance on porcelain conveys auspicious wishes for long life, harmony, and transcendence, while also evoking one of the best-loved legends in Chinese cultural tradition. The present lot may have been used during the Mid-Autumn moon festival when osmanthus wine was traditionally consumed. 

Compare with a related blue and white ewer and cover, Kangxi, decorated with scenes from the Romance of the Western Chamber, illustrated in Kangxi Porcelain Wares from the Shanghai Museum Collection, Hong Kong, 1998, p.76, no.49.

A BLUE AND WHITE 'HAN XIN' PEAR-SHAPED VASE
Kangxi
Elegantly potted with an ovoid body rising from a short foot to a high cylindrical neck, flaring at the mouth, painted around the body in a rich cobalt-blue with a continuous scene of Han Xin and companion riding whilst being chased by Xiao He riding at full gallop before an attendant observing from a gate, Han Xin looking out across the river to see an approaching boatman, all within a landscape of craggy rocks and overhanging pines, a herring-bone border under the mouth rim. 21.5cm (8 1/2in) high.

清康熙 青花蕭何月下追韓信圖長頸瓶 

Han Xin 韓信 (died 196 BC) was a military general who served Liu Bang 劉邦 (died 195 BC) in founding the Han dynasty. Initially, Liu Bang was not impressed with Han Xin and put him in charge of food supplies. This dissatisfied Han Xin who attempted to desert under the cover of darkness. Xiao He 蕭何 (died 193 BC), one of Liu Bang's chief advisers, upon hearing he had left, pursued Han Xin to bring him back, ultimately resulting in Xiao's promotion to the rank of general. According to some versions of the story, Xiao He was unable to catch up to Han Xin because the rise in water level prevented Han from crossing the river. In the Jin dynasty, Jin Renjie wrote the play 'Xiao He Chasing after Han Xin under the Moon' in which Xiao He invited Han Xin for a boat ride after catching up with him; several other Ming dynasty versions of the story also existed.

The original story, recorded in Sima Qian's Shiji (史記), would have resonated strongly with many scholar-officials during the late Ming dynasty, who felt their talents to serve in the government were not being appreciated under the waning Ming empire. The same motif can be found on a baluster vase, c.1635-40, illustrated in Seventeenth Century Chinese Porcelain from the Butler Family Collection, Alexandria, 1990, p.78, no.37. 

See a similar blue and white pear-shaped vase, Kangxi, illustrated in The Frick Collection: An Illustrated Catalogue, vol.VII (Porcelains), New York, 1974, pp.30-31. See also a very similar blue and white vase, with the same design, Kangxi, illustrated in Folklore in Ming and Qing Porcelain, Hong Kong, 2019, pp.48-49.

This work depicts the theme of 'Visiting a Friend with a Qin' (携琴訪友), a timeless subject in Chinese art. According to legend, during the Spring and Autumn period, the musician Boya regarded Zhong Ziqi as his closest friend. When Boya played the piece 'High Mountains and Flowing Water' (高山流水), Zhong Ziqi was able to understand the profound meaning of the music. Their friendship thus became celebrated as the ideal of zhiyin (a person who truly understands another's heart). The theme of Boya carrying his qin, accompanied by a young attendant, to visit his friend was transmitted through the generations and became an enduring pictorial theme in Chinese art.

David David-Weill (1871–1952) was a French banker, philanthropist and prominent collector of Asian art. Born in San Francisco to French parents, he became chairman of Lazard Frères in Paris and assembled an important collection of Chinese bronzes, jades, sculpture, ceramics and cloisonné, acquiring works from leading dealers including C.T.Loo. In 1934 he participated in the Karlbeck Syndicate, an international consortium of museums and private collectors formed to acquire works assembled by the Swedish connoisseur Orvar Karlbeck. A major benefactor of French museums, David-Weill served as president of the Council of the French National Museums from 1925 to 1939 and vice-president of the Société des Amis du Louvre. He lent twelve ancient Chinese bronzes to the International Exhibition of Chinese Art at the Royal Academy, London, in 1935–1936.

The Bactrian camel, capable of carrying heavy loads and enduring extremes of heat and cold, was an essential means of transport along the Central Asian routes linking northern China with the Western Regions. Its appearance in Northern Wei tomb sculpture reflects the increasing movement of foreign merchants, goods and, presumably, Buddhist missionaries along these routes. Camel figures became an established element of Northern Wei funerary assemblages, where they are typically depicted as pack animals carrying saddles, baskets or other loads. As mingqi (明器), such figures served a funerary purpose, providing the deceased with transport and access to the exotic goods associated with elite life.

The present painting is a fine example of the work of Chow Kwa (active mid-19th century), one of the leading artists of the China Trade. Also known as Su Zhaocheng (蘇兆成), Chow Kwa maintained a studio on Park Lane and later on Hankow Road in Shanghai.

The view depicts the embanked quayside of the Bund, extending from the British Consulate at one end to the French Concession at the other. The Huangpu River is populated by a variety of vessels, including American and British steamers, Chinese junks, tanka boats, sampans and barges, while the waterfront is shown with considerable topographical detail. Several features help to establish the date of the composition at around 1857. Most notably, the Wills Bridge, visible at the far right spanning Soochow Creek, was completed in October 1856, while other identifiable buildings and structures provide further evidence for a date in the later 1850s.

For a similar view of the Bund, see P.Conner, Paintings of the China Trade: The Sze Yuan Tang Collection of Historic Paintings, Hong Kong, 2013, p.51, no.38.

This rare and ethereal view depicts Golden Island, or Golden Mountain (Jinshan), known for its rich artistic and literary associations. It was a favoured retreat of the Qianlong Emperor, who composed poetry as well as brought portions of his painting collection to view during his visits there. During his first Southern Tour in 1751, a temporary palace was created on the island. In his poem, First Ascending Jinshan: two poems, the Emperor describes it thus:

亭台俯瞰真无地，星斗平临别有天。
万古豪吟谁造极，一时胜览若登仙

Which may be translated:

Pavilions and terraces overlook, truly no ground beneath,
Stars and constellations level with the eyes, another sky revealed.
Throughout ten thousand ages, who has reached the peak of poetry?
This moment's wondrous view feels like ascending to Immortality.

Members of the Macartney Embassy of 1793 are recorded to have passed by the island, with Sir George Staunton having written 'it belongs to the Emperor, who had built upon it a large and handsome palace, and on the highest eminence several temples and pagodas. The island also contained a large monastery of priests, by whom it is chiefly inhabited' (An Authentic Account of an Embassy, vol.2, London, 1798, p.424). It was later photographed by John Thomson (China and Its People in Early Photographs, vol.III, London, 1873-1874, pl.IX) by which time the buildings had been damaged. An earlier painting of Golden Island is illustrated in Martyn Gregory, Catalogue 64, London, 1994, no.108.

Embroidered on the front and back with eight medallions, each enclosing a crane amidst peaches, prunus blossoms, and butterflies in shades of white, blue, pink and green, reserved on a vivid red ground, all above a terrestrial diagram and wide lishui border at the hem, the cuffs and collar decorated with the 'Eight Daoist Emblems' (anbaxian), lingzhi clouds and shou roundels against a black ground.

The present lot brings together a rich compound of auspicious motifs. In Ming and Qing official dress, the crane motif was originally used for the rank badges of first-rank civil officials. In civilian dress and women's garments, however, the roundel enclosing a crane was employed primarily as an auspicious symbol, expressing wishes for health, longevity, and good fortune. The Daoist emblems adorning the collar and cuffs are known as the 'Eight Hidden Immortals' (暗八仙 anbaxian), referring to the attributes traditionally associated with the Eight Immortals. As the Eight Immortals themselves are symbolised through their implements rather than being depicted directly, the decoration is hence termed as 'hidden'.

See a similar red-ground woman's kesi robe decorated with crane medallions, 19th century, in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (acc.no.49.32.125). See also a similar woman's kesi-woven silk robe, late 19th century, which was sold at Bonhams San Francisco, 21 June 2011, lot 8244. Compare also with a related embroidered red silk woman's informal robe decorated with crane roundels, late Qing dynasty, which was sold at Christie's New York, 23 March 2018, lot 986.
